AN EMPRESS, A FOOTBALL GAME HIJACKED BY HEIDI, A ROBOT ON THE MOON, A UFO OVER ALASKA & A REVOLUTION THAT TURNED VELVET INTO HISTORY!  🫣

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

THE WEIRDEST EVENTS IN HISTORY 🤯

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

STRANGER THAN FICTION — NOVEMBER 17 EDITION

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🕒 ESTIMATED READING TIME: 12 MINUTES

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🗺️ CONSPECTUS

📜 EPIGRAPH — A little truth to set the tone.

🎬 INTRO — Five stories. One very strange date.

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY — Test your instincts.

⭐️ MAIN EVENTS — Five moments when history got spectacularly weird.

🎙️ HARVEY’S CORNER — The rest of the story.

⚖️ CLOSING — The day, considered.

✅ QUIZ ANSWER — The answer revealed.

🍬 CANDY — One last sweet bite, with a look at tomorrow.

💋 SEND-OFF — Pass the madness along.

📣 THERE’S MORE HISTORY WAITING! — The daily lineup.

📚 SOURCES & FURTHER READING — Follow the evidence.

✒️ PUDD’NHEAD WILSON HAS THE LAST WORD — Mark Twain gets the final say.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

📜 EPIGRAPH

“Truth is stranger than fiction, but it is because Fiction is obliged to stick to possibilities; Truth isn't.” ~ Mark Twain, Following the Equator (1897).  ☄️

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🎬 INTRO

What do an empress with her own personal armada, a football game ruined by a little girl, and a machine out for a leisurely stroll on the Moon have in common? Besides a complete absence of adult supervision, they all share a date that clearly never got the memo about behaving normally.

But wait, there’s more, as the infomercials say. A crew of seasoned airline pilots meets something above the last frontier that refuses to fit into any explanation, and trust me, they tried them all. Thousands of students take to the streets and help change the fate of an entire nation, because apparently that’s what happens when young people get fed up and decide they've had enough. And somewhere far from all the chaos, a young mechanic with more grit than cash is about to start a journey that will change transportation forever. Broke, stubborn, and unstoppable, which is a terrible combination for the rest of us.

A television network commits a blunder so spectacular it deserves its own parade. November 17 didn’t just show up; it brought a whole cast of lunatics, geniuses, and unanswered questions.

Five extraordinary events. One remarkable inventor. And enough historical mischief to make fiction pack its bags and go home in shame.

Cue the chaos. Let's roll. 💥

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY

On November 17, 1968, millions of American television viewers missed one of the most extraordinary finishes in professional football history.

What caused them to miss it?

[A] A nationwide electrical blackout.

[B] A children's movie replaced the live broadcast before the game ended.

[C] A technical failure destroyed the television transmission.

[D] The network accidentally broadcast a different game.

👇 (Answer at the end of the issue.)

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

⭐️ MAIN EVENTS

🚢 1869 — THE CANAL, THE EMPRESS & THE FLOATING PARADE

November 17, 1869 | Port Said, Egypt

After ten years of construction, the Suez Canal was officially inaugurated, connecting the Mediterranean and Red Seas and transforming the route between Europe and Asia.

The ceremony was an international spectacle attended by approximately 6,000 guests, including monarchs, diplomats, aristocrats, and cultural figures. Among the most prominent was Empress Eugénie of France, wife of Napoleon III, who arrived aboard the imperial yacht L’Aigle, which was meant to lead the procession of vessels into the new waterway.

Egypt’s Khedive Ismail had invested heavily in presenting his country as a modern power. The canal was both an engineering achievement and a declaration of commercial ambition: ships could now avoid the lengthy journey around Africa’s southern tip.

The project had required enormous excavation and difficult working conditions. Its opening changed international transportation and made the waterway one of the world’s most strategically important passages.

🧩 TRIVIA: The project required the removal of approximately 74 million cubic metres (96.8 million cubic yards) of soil. Its execution cost reached 433 million francs, about twice the initial estimate.

🌀 OBSCURE: L’Aigle was supposed to lead the ceremonial procession, but Captain George Nares, commanding HMS Newport, had other ideas. Under cover of total darkness, without lights, he maneuvered his ship through the waiting vessels and made it through the canal ahead of the imperial yacht. Although the maneuver earned him an official reprimand, it also gave the British commander a rather cheeky place in the canal's history.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The canal changed the geography of commerce. Sometimes human ambition begins by refusing to accept the boundaries nature appears to have established.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

📺 1968 — THE DAY HEIDI STOLE A FOOTBALL GAME

November 17, 1968 | Oakland, California, United States

Imagine watching an important football game, waiting for the final seconds, and suddenly finding yourself watching a children's movie instead. Millions of American viewers experienced precisely that.

The New York Jets were playing the Oakland Raiders. With 65 seconds remaining, the Jets led 32–29. NBC had scheduled a television adaptation of Heidi to begin at a fixed time, and the network switched away from the game.

There was just one problem: the game wasn't over.
Oakland scored a touchdown to take the lead. Then the Jets fumbled the ensuing kickoff, and Oakland recovered and scored again. Two touchdowns in the final nine seconds gave the Raiders a 43–32 victory.

Millions of viewers missed the finish. NBC's telephone lines were overwhelmed by furious callers, and the network apologized. The incident became known as the Heidi Game and helped change how broadcasters handled live sporting events.

🧩 TRIVIA: The game featured ten future Pro Football Hall of Famers. It was already a remarkable contest before the broadcast disaster made it legendary.

🐶 SPOT: The incident became a lasting lesson in live television scheduling. NBC's predetermined programming plan had taken priority over the final seconds of a major sporting event. After the uproar, broadcasters took steps to ensure that scheduled entertainment would not again automatically displace a live game.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A network can control its programming schedule, but it cannot control what happens in the final seconds of a football game.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🌕 1970 — THE FIRST WHEELED VISITOR TO ANOTHER WORLD

November 17, 1970 | Mare Imbrium, Moon

A Soviet spacecraft delivered Lunokhod 1 to the lunar surface, making it the first successful wheeled rover to operate on another celestial body.

The Luna 17 mission landed in the Sea of Rains. After descending from its landing platform, the eight-wheeled vehicle rolled onto the Moon and began photographing the landscape, examining the soil, and conducting scientific experiments.

Operators on Earth guided the rover across unfamiliar terrain, using images and data sent back from the lunar surface. The task demanded careful remote control over a vast distance, with communication delays making the work anything but simple.

Lunokhod's planned operational life was three lunar days—about 21 Earth days. Instead, it functioned for 322 days, travelled approximately 10.5 kilometres, and sent back thousands of images and valuable scientific information.

The little machine helped turn the Moon from a place humans could visit into a place robotic explorers could investigate.

🧩 TRIVIA: Lunokhod 1 weighed approximately 756 kilograms and had eight independently driven wheels. Its design allowed it to negotiate obstacles and travel across terrain that would have challenged a conventional vehicle.

🔑 ESOTERIC: The rover carried a French-built laser reflector containing 14 prisms. Scientists on Earth later used laser pulses directed at the reflector to measure the Earth–Moon distance with remarkable precision. A small robotic explorer was helping measure the distance between two worlds.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Exploration does not always require a human being to take the first step. Sometimes a machine can go where its creators cannot—and send back knowledge for the next journey.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🛸 1986 — THE UFO THAT FOLLOWED A JUMBO JET

November 17, 1986 | Above Alaska, United States

Commercial pilots are trained to recognize aircraft, weather phenomena, and potential hazards. But what happens when experienced flight crew members report something they cannot identify?

The crew of Japan Airlines Flight 1628 encountered an extraordinary situation while flying a Boeing 747 cargo aircraft over Alaska. Captain Kenju Terauchi and his two fellow crew members reported unusual lights accompanying their aircraft.

The flight was travelling from Iceland toward Tokyo, with a stop in Anchorage. Over Alaska, the crew observed lights that appeared to move alongside the jet. Terauchi described two smaller illuminated objects and another enormous object that seemed to follow the aircraft.

The crew reported that the lights remained visible as the aircraft changed course and contacted air traffic controllers. The incident attracted attention because the witnesses were professional pilots, not casual observers.

The Federal Aviation Administration investigated, interviewing the crew and examining radar records and communications. The investigation did not establish that an unidentified craft had accompanied the Boeing 747.

The FAA could not confirm what the crew had witnessed. The pilots’ account nevertheless became one of the most discussed aviation UFO incidents of the 1980s.

🧩 TRIVIA: All three crew members—Captain Terauchi, First Officer Takanori Tamefuji, and Flight Engineer Yoshio Tsukuda—were interviewed by FAA investigators. The agency’s records included pilot interviews, controller communications, and radar information.

🕵️ MYSTERY: What did the crew actually see? The crew were experienced professionals, and FAA investigators found them rational and sober. The FAA still could not confirm that an unidentified craft accompanied the jet. The radar return that seemed to show a second object was a split return from the 747 itself, but that explains the radar image, not the lights the crew saw.

Skeptic Philip Klass argued that the lights were the planets Jupiter and Mars low on the horizon, possibly distorted by ice crystals in the cold air. The crew rejected that explanation, and the FAA never settled the question.

What is known: three pilots reported something they could not identify. What is uncertain: whether it was misidentified planets, an atmospheric effect, or something else.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: An unexplained sighting is not proof of an extraterrestrial visitor. A careful investigation distinguishes what witnesses reported, what instruments recorded, and what the evidence can establish.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🕯️ 1989 — THE VELVET REVOLUTION BEGINS

November 17, 1989 | Prague, Czechoslovakia

Some revolutions begin with armies and declarations of war. Others begin with students carrying banners and hoping their country might someday become free.

Thousands of students gathered in Prague to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the Nazi suppression of Czech universities. In November 1939, occupation authorities had closed the universities, arrested students, sent more than a thousand to concentration camps, and executed nine student leaders.

The 1989 demonstration was initially authorized as a commemorative march. But the peaceful procession became an expression of opposition to the communist government. Police blocked the route and attacked demonstrators on Národní Street. Hundreds were injured.

The crackdown shocked the public and helped ignite a much wider movement. Students organized strikes, theater performers joined the demonstrations, and citizens increasingly filled the streets. The Civic Forum emerged as an opposition movement, and negotiations led to the end of communist rule.

By December, playwright and dissident Václav Havel had become president. The largely peaceful transition became known as the Velvet Revolution.

🧩 TRIVIA: November 17 was designated International Students' Day in 1941, commemorating the Nazi crackdown on Czech students in 1939.

🐶 SPOT: The police assault did not immediately overthrow the government. Its importance lay in the public reaction: a student protest became a national movement as ordinary citizens recognized the attack as an assault on their own freedom.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A government can suppress a demonstration, but it cannot always suppress the determination that brought people into the streets.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🎙️ HARVEY’S CORNER

🔧 SOICHIRO HONDA — THE BOY WHO TURNED A BICYCLE INTO A DREAM

Good day, everybody.

Some people see a machine and admire what it can do. Others immediately wonder how it works—and how to make it work better. Soichiro Honda belonged firmly in the second category.

Born November 17, 1906, in Komyo Village, Japan, he was the eldest son of a blacksmith and a weaver. His father, Gihei, was skilled at working with metal and also operated a bicycle shop. His mother, Mika, was an accomplished weaver. Their household was not wealthy, but practical craftsmanship was part of everyday life.

Honda's fascination with machinery began early. An automobile passing through his village made a lasting impression. He never forgot the smell of its oil. At fifteen, he left home for Tokyo and became an apprentice at the Art Shokai automobile repair shop.

He learned by doing: repairing engines, working on vehicles, and developing a reputation for mechanical ingenuity. But he was interested in more than repairing other people's machines.

While still an apprentice, he helped his employers, the Sakakibara brothers, build a racing car called the Curtiss. Its engine had originally powered an American Curtiss Jenny biplane and was fitted into the chassis of a Mitchell automobile. On November 23, 1924, the machine won the Fifth Japan Motor Car Championship, with Honda serving as its riding mechanic.

Imagine that: a teenager helping put an aircraft engine into a car and then taking it racing. Apparently, ordinary transportation had never held much appeal for him.

In 1928, Honda completed his apprenticeship and was entrusted with opening an Art Shokai branch in Hamamatsu. He eventually established his own manufacturing venture, Tokai Seiki, with a determination to produce automobile piston rings.

But his first attempts were anything but successful.

His early piston rings suffered from serious technical problems. Honda discovered that practical mechanical ability alone wasn't enough to master the science of manufacturing. Rather than pretend he knew everything, he enrolled in technical studies to improve his understanding of metallurgy.

The effort paid off, but the road remained difficult. When he submitted fifty piston rings to Toyota for quality inspection, only three met the required standards.

Three out of fifty.

Most people might have considered that a reason to abandon the project. Honda considered it a reason to learn more. He visited universities and steelmaking companies, studied manufacturing techniques, and kept experimenting until he could produce components that met the necessary standards.

His company eventually became a major supplier, employing more than 2,000 people at its height.

Then came the war.

Air raids destroyed Tokai Seiki's Yamashita plant, and an earthquake in January 1945 brought down another factory. The business Honda had worked so hard to build was devastated. He eventually sold his interest in the company and began considering what to do next.

Postwar Japan faced enormous shortages, including a desperate need for affordable transportation. Bicycles were among the most important means of getting around, but even those could be difficult to use when carrying heavy loads.

Honda saw an opportunity.

In September 1946, he established the Honda Technical Research Institute. Around that time, he encountered a small surplus engine originally designed to power a wireless radio generator for the former Imperial Japanese Army.

An idea immediately came to him: why not use the engine to power a bicycle?

He acquired approximately 500 of the engines and began adapting them for civilian transportation.

But he didn't simply bolt an engine onto a bicycle and send it out the door. His first experimental arrangement used a friction roller against the front wheel, but the poor-quality tires of the period wore out quickly. He abandoned that approach and developed a more practical belt-driven arrangement.

There was even a wonderfully improvised touch: one early prototype used a Japanese hot-water bottle as its fuel tank.

That's ingenuity with whatever happens to be lying around!

Honda also insisted on quality. He dismantled, refined, and reassembled each engine, then tested the finished bicycle before it reached a customer. The resulting motorized bicycles became popular, offering people a relatively inexpensive way to travel.

But Honda knew the supply of surplus engines wouldn't last forever. He began developing an engine of his own, and in November 1947 introduced the A-Type auxiliary bicycle engine, his first original product.

In September 1948, he founded Honda Motor Co., Ltd. with Takeo Fujisawa, a business partner whose commercial and organizational abilities complemented Honda's engineering imagination.

It was a partnership that mattered enormously. Honda brought technical creativity and an appetite for experimentation; Fujisawa helped build the business capable of turning those ideas into a lasting enterprise.

The company grew from its humble beginnings in Hamamatsu into one of the world's leading motorcycle manufacturers. It later expanded into automobiles and international motorsport, earning a global reputation for engineering, performance, and innovation.

Honda eventually retired from the company's presidency but remained an influential figure. He died on August 5, 1991, aged 84.

Consider the journey: a blacksmith's son leaves home as a teenager, becomes a mechanic, helps build an aircraft-engine racing car, struggles with manufacturing failures, studies metallurgy, loses the factories he worked so hard to establish, and starts again by adapting surplus engines to bicycles.

That is not a conventional corporate success story. It is perseverance with a toolbox.

And perhaps the most remarkable part is that Honda never seemed satisfied with simply making something work. He wanted to understand why it worked, how it could work better, and how it could make life easier for somebody else.

The boy who once watched an automobile pass through his village helped build a company whose machines would eventually travel around the world.

And now, you know the rest of the story.

—— ❧ ——

NOTICE & TRIBUTE: “Harvey’s Corner” is an original historical feature inspired by the storytelling tradition of legendary radio broadcaster Paul Harvey (1918–2009). This independent editorial homage is not affiliated with, sponsored by, or endorsed by the Paul Harvey estate or ABC Radio.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

⚖️ CLOSING

November 17 reminds us that history rarely follows a predictable script.

The Suez Canal reshaped global commerce. The Heidi Game showed how one scheduling decision could become a national television disaster. Lunokhod 1 proved that machines could explore another world. The Alaska encounter remains a debated aviation mystery, while the Velvet Revolution demonstrated how students and ordinary citizens could help transform a nation.

And Soichiro Honda's life offers a lesson of its own: failure need not end an ambition. It can become the reason to learn more, experiment again, and find another way forward.

Sometimes history changes because someone builds a canal. Sometimes because a television network starts a movie too early. Sometimes because a small machine begins rolling across the Moon. And sometimes because students refuse to remain silent.

And as if November 17 hadn't already accomplished enough, there's one more little milestone hiding in the date: in 1970, Douglas Engelbart received the patent for his computer pointing device—the invention that would become the computer mouse. Apparently, even the mouse wanted its moment in history. 🖱️

As for Heidi, she may have been an innocent little girl in the Swiss Alps, but American football fans have never quite forgiven her.  🤭

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

✅ QUIZ ANSWER: [B] A children's movie replaced the live broadcast before the game ended.

NBC switched from the Jets–Raiders game with 65 seconds remaining. Oakland scored twice in the final nine seconds and won 43–32. Millions of viewers missed the finish, and television broadcasting history was never quite the same.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🍬 CANDY

Tomorrow, history has another collection of surprises waiting. Somewhere between ambition and absurdity, an ordinary situation will take an extraordinary turn—and someone will discover that the past has a peculiar sense of timing.

No names. No spoilers. Just a little mystery to keep the curiosity alive.

Until then, stay curious. The next strange chapter is already waiting.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

💋 SEND-OFF

If today's stories made you smile, think, or wonder how any of this actually happened, pass them along.

Share the strange, challenge the familiar, and keep asking questions. History is far too interesting to leave sitting quietly on a shelf.

Until next time, keep your curiosity sharp—and if you're watching a football game, remember to keep an eye on the television schedule. Heidi may be waiting in the wings.

▫️𝗞𝗲𝗻𝗻𝘆 𝗚𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘄𝗲𝗹𝗹, TB (@ DET)

Gainwell has totaled at least 76 yards in each of his last three games, averaging 101 yards during that stretch. A matchup with Detroit always has the potential to turn into a track meet.

▫️𝗞𝗮𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗻 𝗕𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗸, SF (vs. MIN)

Black has carved out a weekly role on the league's best offense. San Francisco is committed to preserving CMC, and if he misses time, Black immediately becomes a top-10 RB. He should be rostered in EVERY league.

▫️𝗦𝗲𝘁𝗵 𝗠𝗰𝗚𝗼𝘄𝗮𝗻, IND (@ HOU)

Plenty of managers dropped McGowan after Jonathan Taylor wasn't traded, but he still has a legitimate role. With the Colts potentially facing a lost season, there's a chance Taylor could be shut down late in the year.

▫️𝗝𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗛𝗶𝗹𝗹, BAL (@ CAR)

Baltimore's season hit a low point with its loss to the previously winless Chargers. 

Hill's speed and pass-catching ability are things this offense needs, and this backfield is more of a timeshare than most realize. Excellent matchup against Carolina.

𝗪𝗜𝗗𝗘 𝗥𝗘𝗖𝗘𝗜𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗦 🎯

▫️𝗧𝗿𝗲 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗶𝘀, LAC (vs. NYJ)

Ladd McConkey's injury struggles continue, and Harris is taking advantage. 

He played nearly every snap in Week 10 and accounted for 67% of the team's receiving yards. Great matchup ahead for an ascending young player.

▫️𝗣𝗮𝘁 𝗕𝗿𝘆𝗮𝗻𝘁, DEN (vs. LV)

Bryant has been effective when on the field for Denver and should be heavily involved going forward now that he's healthy again.

▫️𝗔𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗶𝗼 𝗪𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗺𝘀, WAS (vs. CIN)

Williams continues to lead Washington's receivers in snaps since Terry McLaurin went down. 

A potential shootout against Cincinnati gives him an opportunity to deliver another useful fantasy performance.

▫️𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗯 𝗗𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗹𝗮𝘀, MIA (@ BUF)

We don't care what the situation looks like when the fantasy points keep coming. Douglas has emerged as Miami's best WR and should see plenty of volume against Buffalo. 

He's topped 70 yards in three of his last four games and brings legitimate big-play ability.

▫️𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸 𝗔𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗲𝘄𝘀, BAL (@ CAR)

Right around the 50% ownership cutoff, Andrews is a priority add if available. New Ravens QB Jacoby Brissett peppered him with targets in his debut and has historically loved targeting tight ends. Go get him!

Brock Bowers could miss time with an ankle injury. Mayer is already playing nearly every snap, but would become a focal point of the passing game for Fernando Mendoza if Bowers is sidelined.

A potential shootout with Cincinnati on Monday night gives Okonkwo an opportunity. He has the big-play ability to take advantage, and the Bengals have been one of the league's worst defenses against tight ends.

text:
Is there a worse contract in the NFL right now than DK Metcalf’s?

If the Steelers were to cut Metcalf today, they’d reportedly be on the hook for around $36 million.

And based on his production this season, it’s getting harder to justify that investment.

Metcalf hasn’t looked anything like a legitimate number one wide receiver. Most weeks, he’s producing more like a number two or even number three option.

His 15.4% drop rate is the worst of his career.

He dropped another pass against Cincinnati, and just two weeks earlier against Cleveland, one of his drops turned into an interception.

But here’s what really caught my attention.

Lately, we’ve seen the Steelers try to force-feed Metcalf the football late in games, often when the outcome is already decided.

So I went back and looked at his production without those garbage-time receptions.

Through nine games, here’s what you’re left with:

30 receptions. 339 receiving yards.

That’s an average of just three catches for 37 yards per game.

For a player carrying that kind of financial commitment, that’s nowhere near good enough.

The Steelers brought Metcalf in to be a difference-maker. Someone who could elevate the passing game and give Aaron Rodgers a legitimate number one target.

Instead, he’s been inconsistent, struggled with drops, and failed to deliver the production this offense desperately needs.

At some point, we have to ask whether the Steelers are getting anything close to what they’re paying for.

Because right now, I don’t think they are.

This is from a civilian, dumbfuck. Read it again! 

Furthermore, learn what that patch represents:

Pilots and engineers apply for Test Pilot School entirely by choice, and transitioning into the flight test community is a voluntary career track.
To even be considered for the U.S. Air Force Test Pilot School (USAF TPS) or the U.S. Naval Test Pilot School (USNTPS), service members must actively submit an application package, meet strict engineering and flight-hour prerequisites, and compete before a selection board.
When they enter this track, they voluntarily make a few key career trade-offs:

 Attending TPS is an expensive, year-long investment for the military. Graduates incur an Active Duty Service Commitment (usually three to four years) specifically to pay back that training by working in flight test.

 Rather than returning to standard front-line combat or operational flying units, graduates are assigned to developmental test wings (like Edwards AFB, Eglin AFB, or NAS Patuxent River). Their daily job shifts from combat readiness to flying experimental aircraft, testing new weapons systems, and writing technical reports.

 While the flight test community offers incredible opportunities—including being the primary pipeline for military NASA astronauts and senior acquisition leaders—stepping out of traditional operational leadership tracks can sometimes mean giving up conventional command paths in standard flying squadrons.

Most pilots who pursue TPS do so because they love engineering, want to push the boundaries of aviation, or aspire to become astronauts or program managers for future aircraft.

text:
$NVDA $TSM TSMC AND NVIDIA: THE DIVISION OF LABOR AFTER THE JENSEN TRANSITION

The most critical operational learning from NVIDIA's Q3 FY27 earnings call on 11/17/26 was not a number. It was a name: TSMC.

THE TELL FROM THE CALL

Answering Vivek Arya's question on what stays durable through the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress said: "I see right now the leadership, even from TSMC, that was in our offices just this week, also fully engaged in helping us. We secured memory. We secured advanced packaging."

The sentence was not in prepared remarks. It was offered, in a governance answer, as evidence that the company's moat survives the founder's exit. Of every institution Kress could have named, she named the foundry, and she named it at the level of "leadership in our offices this week," meaning the engagement is executive to executive during the transition week itself, not a standing purchase order.

The same day, NVIDIA published its supply-chain release, "NVIDIA Expands Commitments With Supply Chain Partners to Support AI Infrastructure Buildout." In it, TSMC SVP and deputy co-COO Dr. Kevin Zhang is quoted: "TSMC and NVIDIA share a longstanding partnership built on semiconductor innovation. This deep collaboration allows us to plan for future technology requirements and prepare our manufacturing capabilities as NVIDIA brings new platforms to market." The release states that Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs began volume shipments in Q3 FY27 leveraging TSMC's 5nm, 3nm, and CoWoS advanced packaging technologies. Zhang is the right name to notice: he is TSMC's senior executive for the technology and packaging side of the customer relationship, and his April 2026 public remarks confirmed TSMC will build advanced packaging capacity (CoWoS and 3D-IC) in Arizona before 2029, moving TSMC from pure wafer foundry toward localized one-stop service for NVIDIA and Apple.

HOW A FOUNDRY CARRIES A FABLESS ROADMAP

TSMC's support for NVIDIA's roadmap is not generic capacity. It operates through five concrete mechanisms.

First, custom process variants built for NVIDIA alone. NVIDIA's own architecture pages state that Blackwell GPUs are "manufactured using a custom-built TSMC 4NP process," and NVIDIA's Hopper technical blog states the GH100 was "fabricated using the TSMC 4N process customized for NVIDIA." 4N was a variant of TSMC's N4 tuned for NVIDIA; 4NP refined it. A foundry does not build a named, customer-specific process flavor for a customer it treats as interchangeable. This is design-technology co-optimization in its most literal form: the process design kit, transistor tuning, and yield learning are accumulated against NVIDIA's reticle-limit dies (Blackwell is two dies, 208 billion transistors), and that accumulated learning is not transferable to another vendor on any useful timeline.

Second, node sequencing locked years ahead. Vera Rubin ships on TSMC 3nm-class process (reported as N3P, a refined 3nm variant, paired with CoWoS-L packaging), with networking and other platform silicon on 5nm. Rubin Ultra follows in 2027. For Feynman (2028), multiple supply-chain reports say NVIDIA will be the first, and reportedly the only, customer for TSMC's A16 node, whose defining feature is Super Power Rail backside power delivery, worth a claimed 8 to 10% speed gain at the same voltage or 15 to 20% power reduction at the same speed against N2P per TSMC's own symposium figures. Apple is reported to skip A16 entirely and go from N2 to A14. The significance for the transition question: the Feynman decision, if the reports are right, was made inside the Huang era and binds NVIDIA to TSMC's most experimental node for 2028. Whoever the permanent CEO is, the silicon roadmap through 2028 is already a TSMC joint program. One counterweight: DigiTimes has reported NVIDIA exploring Intel EMIB packaging for a minority share (reported around 25%) of Feynman packaging, with the balance at TSMC. That reporting is single-source and unconfirmed. Even if true, it diversifies a packaging step, not the wafer or the roadmap relationship.

The CPU leg of the roadmap runs through the same channel. The 11/17/26 release states that Vera CPUs, not only Rubin GPUs, began volume shipments in Q3 FY27 on TSMC process and CoWoS technologies. Management expects standalone CPU revenue to more than double in fiscal 2028 as Vera moves from the Grace pattern (a CPU paired inside a Grace Blackwell or Vera Rubin system) toward a merchant CPU sold across cloud operators and AI customers for agent execution and orchestration workloads. That expansion is entirely fabless: every incremental Vera CPU is a TSMC wafer and, in its packaged form, CoWoS capacity. TSMC's side has publicly leaned into the same theme, with Wei's Q2 2026 call remarks on agentic CPU demand. For the transition question this matters because the CPU is the newest and least Huang-dependent leg of the roadmap: its ramp is a manufacturing and packaging execution problem of exactly the kind TSMC underwrites, rather than a founder-vision problem.

Third, CoWoS allocation as the shipment governor. Advanced packaging, not wafer starts, is the binding constraint on AI accelerator shipments. TSMC's CoWoS capacity ran about 13,000 to 16,000 wafers per month in 2023, about 70,000 by end of 2025, is expected to exceed 130,000 per month by end of 2026, and to reach roughly 170,000 to 200,000 per month in 2027 depending on the estimating house (KGI at 170k, UBS at about 180k for TSMC within a 270k industry total, other supply chain estimates above 200k). Morgan Stanley's supply chain survey puts NVIDIA's share of global CoWoS demand at about 60% in 2026, easing to about 45% in 2027 as hyperscaler ASICs grow; UBS puts NVIDIA's share of CoWoS wafer demand at 65% in 2025 falling to 49% in 2027. NVIDIA is reported to have booked about 595,000 CoWoS wafers for 2026, roughly 515,000 of them from TSMC, the bulk CoWoS-L for Rubin, Vera CPUs, and GB-series parts. One arithmetic tension in the source set: 515,000 wafers against the capacity path above implies roughly 40 to 45% of TSMC's 2026 CoWoS output, below the roughly 60% demand-share survey figure. The two series most likely measure different things (surveyed demand versus booked or allocated wafers), so they should not be combined arithmetically; either way, NVIDIA is the pool's largest single claimant by a wide margin. C.C. Wei has said on an investor call that packaging capacity was "so tight that it limited customer growth." When Kress says "we secured advanced packaging," this is the asset she means: allocation inside a capacity pool that will not clear demand until 2027 at the earliest, allocated by TSMC, to the customer TSMC chooses to prioritize.

Fourth, yield and ramp co-management. Vera Rubin generated nearly $20 billion of revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, the fastest ramp in NVIDIA's history. A ramp of that slope on a new platform, a new memory generation (HBM4), and CoWoS-L packaging is a joint NVIDIA-TSMC engineering exercise: defect density learning on reticle-scale dies, interposer supply (including the GlobalFoundries silicon interposer agreement inside the CoWoS ecosystem), and substrate capacity, which is why the 11/17/26 release also carries Kinsus expanding NVIDIA-dedicated substrate capacity by more than 3.5x and SPIL expanding advanced packaging under multiyear agreement with multibillion-dollar NVIDIA funding. TSMC's role in a ramp is the unglamorous one that decides whether a launch quarter is a beat or a miss: it owns the yield curve.

Fifth, capacity underwriting through prepayment and commitment structures on both sides. NVIDIA's supply commitments rose from $279 billion to $390 billion in one quarter, primarily multi-year memory procurement, inside $518 billion of all-in commitments. On the capital-allocation question, Kress ranked supplier prepaids as the top operating use of capital after buybacks. TSMC's side of the same structure is its capex: the 2026 budget stands at $60 to $64 billion, with Deutsche Bank's October 2026 forecasts putting 2027 capex at $84 billion and 2028 at $100 billion (single-source analyst estimates). Wei's stated discipline is that he verifies demand personally before spending: "I want to make sure that my customers' demand are real. So I talked to those cloud service providers, all of them... they show me the evidence that the AI really helps their business." The mechanism, in one sentence: NVIDIA prepays and commits, TSMC builds and allocates, and each side's balance sheet now carries the other's forecast.

WHAT TSMC HAS AT STAKE

NVIDIA is now TSMC's largest customer. Analyst estimates carried by CNBC in January 2026 put NVIDIA at roughly $33 billion of TSMC revenue in 2026, about 22% of the total, against Apple's roughly $27 billion and 18%, and Huang himself confirmed the ranking on a podcast ("Morris will be happy to know NVIDIA is TSMC's largest customer now"). TSMC does not publish customer-level revenue, so the percentages are estimates, while the ranking is confirmed by Huang's own statement. One vintage warning on those figures: the January 2026 estimates imply a TSMC 2026 revenue total near $150 billion, but TSMC has since blown past that path, with Q3 2026 revenue of about $46.7 billion, Q4 guided to $52.3 to $54.3 billion, and full-year growth guidance raised to around 44%. On the current run rate, $33 billion would be a materially smaller share than 22%, so either the dollar figure is now stale and too low if the share held, or the share has eased as the rest of the HPC complex grew. The ranking is confirmed; the exact 2026 share is not. TSMC's disclosed platform mix shows the concentration underneath: HPC was 68% of revenue in Q3 2026, and NVIDIA is the largest single contributor to that platform.

The Arizona program prices the stake. TSMC's US commitment stood at $165 billion (six fabs, two advanced packaging facilities, an R&D center) after the March 2025 addition of $100 billion. At the Q2 2026 earnings call, Wei announced a further $100 billion US investment, taking the Arizona total to $265 billion across 12 facilities, with dedicated CoWoS packaging capacity in Arizona aimed at the AI packaging bottleneck. Arizona's anchor demand is US AI and HPC customers; the campus exists because NVIDIA-class demand made US leading-edge capacity financeable, and its economics depend on that demand persisting at high utilization for decades. Advanced packaging is becoming a P&L line in its own right: UBS expects advanced packaging and testing to reach about 12% of TSMC's sales in 2026 and 16% in 2027.

The exposure is symmetric and already visible in the tape. On 11/16/26, before NVIDIA had reported anything, Asia sold the supply chain on the NVIDIA CEO story: the Taiex fell 6.03%, its second-largest point drop on record, and TSMC fell 5.74% (exchange figures relayed across multiple accounts; treat as color, consistent across sources). TSMC's equity is, in part, a derivative of NVIDIA's stability. If NVIDIA stumbles, TSMC does not merely lose orders: it holds CoWoS capacity built for one customer's package architecture, N3 and A16 capacity sequenced around one customer's roadmap, and an Arizona gigafab cluster whose utilization case is AI demand concentrated in a handful of US customers, NVIDIA first among them. Wei's own hedge is the rest of the HPC complex (AMD, Broadcom, the hyperscaler ASIC programs all ride the same CoWoS pool, which is why NVIDIA's share falls toward 45 to 49% by 2027 even as its absolute wafers grow), plus Apple on the consumer side. But there is no second NVIDIA: no other customer accounts for roughly 60% of global CoWoS demand in the Morgan Stanley survey or anchors a custom-node program.

This is the factual core underneath the claim that "they won't let $1tr of new fabs get mothballed." The trillion-dollar figure is best understood at industry scale rather than as a TSMC line item: announced US semiconductor investment since 2020 exceeds $828 billion across 160 projects (Semiconductor Industry Association figures), TSMC's own Arizona program is $265 billion, and TSMC's annual capex is on a path from $60 to $64 billion in 2026 toward a Deutsche Bank-estimated $100 billion by 2028. The fab complex being built on the assumption of NVIDIA-shaped demand is, in aggregate, of the order named. The incentive conclusion follows from the arithmetic, not from sentiment: TSMC's return on this buildout requires NVIDIA to keep shipping, so TSMC's rational move in a NVIDIA leadership crisis is exactly what Kress described, maximum engagement, senior people in the room, capacity and engineering support visibly committed.

TESTING THE DIVISION OF LABOR

The framing: TSMC underwrites the silicon side (process, packaging, manufacturing engineering, roadmap execution support) while NVIDIA's executive attention concentrates on land, power, and shell (neocloud financing, guarantees, prepaids, allocation by site readiness).

WHERE IT HOLDS

The call's own evidence sorts mostly along this line, with one correction. The TSMC facts Kress offered were leadership engaged and packaging secured, plus Rubin ramping at a record pace on TSMC 5nm, 3nm, and CoWoS. Memory is not a TSMC fact: TSMC does not supply HBM. NVIDIA secures HBM from its memory vendors separately (the $390 billion supply-commitment jump was primarily multi-year memory procurement), and TSMC's role is to integrate that HBM into the package through CoWoS. Conflating the two overstates TSMC's remit; the accurate claim is that TSMC underwrites the logic dies and the packaging into which separately secured memory is assembled. Every hard fact about NVIDIA's own executive work on the call was an infrastructure fact: $390 billion of supply commitments, $518 billion all-in, up to $118 billion of guarantee exposure dominated by $105 billion of SB Energy credit support, and the allocation answer, in which NVIDIA allocates its scarce output by the customer's land, power, and shell readiness and capital readiness, at uniform pricing. NVIDIA is behaving, at the top of the house, like the underwriter and allocator of an infrastructure buildout; TSMC is behaving like the guarantor of the silicon roadmap underneath it. The FY28 outlook raise to about 75% growth, delivered by an interim CEO six days into the job, is only credible if the supply side is someone else's solved problem; Kress's TSMC sentence is where she told you whose.

WHERE IT OVERSTATES

Three corrections. First, the silicon side is not outsourced in the way the framing can imply: NVIDIA still designs everything. The architectures (Rubin, Rubin Ultra, Feynman), the Vera CPU, the NVLink and networking roadmap (networking revenue above $21 billion in Q3), and the platform definitions are NVIDIA's, and TSMC has no ability to originate them. What TSMC underwrites is manufacturability and execution: that a designed part can be built, at yield, at volume, on schedule. Second, TSMC's engagement is not NVIDIA-specific charity; it is the foundry model working as designed for its largest customer, and the same CoWoS pool serves Broadcom, AMD, and the ASIC programs that compete with NVIDIA. TSMC will guarantee the ship is steady because the ship is roughly a fifth of its revenue on the January-vintage estimates, not because it has adopted NVIDIA's strategy. Third, the division is not new this week. The 4N custom process dates to Hopper (2022); what changed on 11/17/26 is that NVIDIA's interim leadership said the quiet part on an earnings call, because for the first time the question "who holds this company together operationally" was asked in public and the honest answer had a name.

WHAT TSMC CANNOT REPLACE

• CUDA and the software stack. The moat is a developer ecosystem, not a process node; TSMC has no software business.
• Systems architecture: NVL72 rack-scale design, NVLink fabric, the Spectrum and ConnectX networking line, and the CPU-GPU platform integration that makes Vera Rubin a system rather than a chip.
• Product definition and pricing: the allocation and uniform-pricing decisions Kress described are commercial acts only NVIDIA can perform.
• Customer and ecosystem capital: the guarantees, prepaids, and neocloud support structures are NVIDIA balance-sheet instruments TSMC neither offers nor could credibly replicate.
• Demand creation itself: TSMC sells capacity to whoever designs winning silicon; it cannot make the market want NVIDIA's.

If NVIDIA's design organization faltered, TSMC's capacity would migrate to AMD, Broadcom, and the hyperscaler ASICs within a few quarters, which is precisely the limit of the "taking over from the inside" thesis: TSMC can keep NVIDIA's roadmap manufacturable through a transition, and it has every incentive to, but it cannot be NVIDIA.

One further limit cuts the other way, against NVIDIA: the division of labor deepens a single-point concentration. Arizona advanced packaging arrives only before 2029 on Zhang's April 2026 remarks, so through the Rubin and Rubin Ultra ramps the CoWoS pool that governs NVIDIA's shipments remains overwhelmingly Taiwan-based. TSMC's engagement removes execution risk from the transition; it does not diversify the geography of the supply chain NVIDIA now depends on more explicitly than before.

VERDICT ON THE THREE CLAIMS

• "It looks like TSMC is taking over from the inside." Overstates if read as control, and is accurate if read as load-bearing: the operational continuity of NVIDIA currently runs through Hsinchu to a degree no other supplier relationship in the industry matches.
• "They won't let $1tr of new fabs get mothballed." Directionally right on incentives and roughly right on scale at industry level.
• "TSMC will guarantee the NVDA ship is steady and moving forward for as long as needed." The strongest of the three as stated: it is exactly what TSMC's revenue concentration, capex commitments, and Kress's account of this week's engagement describe, with one amendment. "For as long as needed" lasts only while NVIDIA keeps designing parts the market wants. The guarantee covers execution, not relevance.

THE REACTION

The TSMC line was extracted from the call within minutes and framed as a headline fact. Nicholas Mugalli (RealNickMugalli) led his call summary: "KRESS REVEALS TSMC LEADERSHIP VISITED NVIDIA'S OFFICES THIS WEEK AND IS FULLY ENGAGED IN SUPPORTING THE TRANSITION (NVDA, TSM)," bundled with "business as usual" and "suppliers and partners 100% behind the company." The Transcript (TheTranscript_) singled the same moment out as a standalone observation: Kress "casually name-dropped that the TSMC leadership was at NVIDIA's offices just this week." The read on X, in other words, matched this one: of everything said on the call, the TSMC sentence was the one the earnings-call transcription community treated as news. Broader post-earnings summaries led with the 75% FY28 raise and the $390 billion commitments rather than the TSMC angle, and the pre-print record shows the other side of the stake, the 11/16/26 Asia selloff on the CEO story. No informed channel source in this sweep contradicted the engagement account; no TSMC-side statement beyond Zhang's release quote has appeared as of this writing. The sweep covered keyword searches on the call window, not an exhaustive timeline pull.

OPEN QUESTIONS

• The exact CoWoS capacity and NVIDIA allocation figures are analyst estimates; TSMC does not disclose them. The 2027 NVIDIA share range (45 to 49%) is a two-house estimate band, not a fact.
• Whether Feynman is in fact an A16 design, and whether any Feynman packaging goes to Intel EMIB, rests on Taiwan supply-chain reporting and one DigiTimes item. NVIDIA and TSMC have not confirmed either.
• The Arizona total: $165 billion is the documented figure; the step to $265 billion rests on Q2 2026 call reporting. TSMC's own release text for the increment was not read firsthand in this research.
• NVIDIA's exact share of TSMC 2026 revenue is unresolved, for the vintage reason given above. The largest-customer ranking is confirmed; the current share is not measured by any source found.
• Whether TSMC's engagement includes any formal engineering secondment or joint task force inside NVIDIA (as distinct from executive visits and standing joint development) is not in any source found; Kress's sentence supports presence and engagement, not an organizational chart.

text:
This week, global business and political leaders are converging in #Shenzhen for a pivotal moment in regional diplomacy. On November 17–18, the #APEC CEO Summit 2026 will open at the Qianhai International Conference Center, setting the stage for the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting on November 18–19. Marking China’s third turn as APEC host—following Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014—and the most significant diplomatic event in the opening year of its 15th Five-Year Plan, the Shenzhen gathering arrives at a critical juncture. For a global economy weighed down by sluggish recovery and geopolitical fragmentation, the meeting offers a timely test of whether the Asia-Pacific can remain a pillar of stability and shared growth.

The central question facing the region is straightforward: where does Asia-Pacific cooperation go from here? Together, APEC's 21 member economies account for more than 60 percent of global GDP and nearly half of world trade, making the region the undisputed engine of global growth. Yet that engine faces growing headwinds—from rising unilateralism and protectionism to the increasing politicization of trade and industrial and supply chains. At such a moment, steering the region toward steady, open cooperation is essential. As the world's second-largest economy, China contributes over 60 percent of Asia-Pacific economic growth and serves as the largest trading partner for 13 APEC member economies. By setting "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together" as the theme for the 2026 APEC "China Year," with "Openness, Innovation, Cooperation" as its three priorities, Beijing is making a clear case against decoupling and zero-sum rivalry.

Perhaps the clearest signal of confidence comes from the private sector, which has voted with its feet. More than 2,000 political and business leaders are attending the APEC CEO Summit 2026, representing all 21 APEC member economies alongside major enterprises from 13 non-APEC economies, including the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Switzerland. Notably, 115 Fortune Global 500 companies are represented in Qianhai—with US firms accounting for nearly 20 percent of participating enterprises from economies other than China, the largest international contingent. That level of turnout underscores a practical reality: multinational businesses still view the Asia-Pacific as indispensable, and they remain eager to tap into the opportunities of China's continuous opening-up and industrial modernization.

Historically, this year's summit also marks an important inflection point. Over the past quarter-century—from the 2001 Shanghai Accord to the 2014 Beijing Agenda and the Beijing Roadmap for APEC's Contribution to the Realization of the FTAAP, which formally launched the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP) process—China’s role within APEC has evolved from participant to agenda-setter. Appropriately, 2026 marks both the 20th anniversary of the FTAAP vision and the final review year of the APEC Connectivity Blueprint for 2015–2025. Rather than settling for broad declarations, the Shenzhen agenda is geared toward concrete deliverables: the CEO Summit will issue the APEC CEO Summit Shenzhen Initiative 2026—the first such outcome document in its 30-year history—while leaders are set to advance practical frameworks for digital trade, cross-border data verification, an open and inclusive AI innovation ecosystem, and the digital and green transition, laying actionable groundwork toward the APEC Putrajaya Vision 2040.

Choosing Shenzhen as the host city carries unmistakable symbolism. Once a quiet coastal town, Shenzhen transformed into a global hub of technology and trade through China’s reform and opening-up—its rise mirroring the broader "Asia-Pacific miracle." Today, anchored by the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area's blend of world-class physical infrastructure and regulatory connectivity, the city serves as a natural bridge between China and the Pacific Rim. The international delegates' firsthand exposure to Shenzhen's tech firms, green industrial parks, and urban dynamism allows the world to see China's innovation-driven growth up close—and turn dialogue into tangible, mutually beneficial partnerships.

Great eras demand broad vision and pragmatic leadership. As leaders gather in Shenzhen, the upcoming summit is both a reaffirmation of China's commitment to high-standard opening-up and a vital opportunity for APEC member economies to rebuild consensus. Guided by the forthcoming Shenzhen Declaration, the region has a chance to choose openness over barriers, innovation over stagnation, and cooperation over division—writing the next chapter of the Asia-Pacific growth story.

GAI DATA CENTER DEVELOPMENT DAILY DIGEST, TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 17, 2026

LEAD ITEMS

- Project Jupiter, Dona Ana County, New Mexico: HSBC sold its roughly $300 million slice of the $18 billion construction financing in the mid-80s, and ING and Societe Generale are reported offering up to $800 million more of data center loans for sale, detailed under FINANCING ITEMS.

NEW LAUNCHES

- Giga Energy Project Clay, Hunt County, Texas, event 11/17/26, verified. Giga Energy will develop, own and operate the approximately 30 acre campus for an undisclosed US based AI cloud provider under a 10 year lease stated at $1 billion; ground was broken in July 2026 and service is expected spring 2027. Capacity is 60 MW, below the 100 MW floor, included under the strategic clause. Naming defect recorded on the finding: Giga issued two releases the same day for the same project, the morning release naming it Project Marl and the later release Project Clay; it is one campus, and the name must be resolved before any census load. The lease is also tonight's pre-leasing pass item, merged into this one finding.

- Lenovo Wanquan Hybrid Token Factory Mother Plant, Zhangjiakou, Hebei, China, LATE, event 11/10/26, verified. Lenovo launched the Wanquan Hybrid Token Factory brand and signed a cooperation agreement with the Zhangjiakou municipal government for the first mother plant: an initial 15,000P heterogeneous computing cluster and an intelligent computing center of about 100 MW, phase 1 construction set for 2027. No district or parcel was published.

- Meridian One, Hickstead, West Sussex, United Kingdom, LATE, event 10/26, month precision only, verified. A proposal for a phased campus at Northlands Enterprise Park with a long-term power ambition of 100 MW, five liquid-cooled buildings and a stated investment ambition above 1 billion pounds over about 10 years. The 100 MW is an ambition figure, not committed capacity, and planning permission has not yet been submitted.

- NorthVault AI campus, Ontario, Canada, event 11/17/26, lead only. A newly launched firm announced an AI campus with 4 MW available now, 43.75 MW to be energized by Q3 2027, and a long-term path to 120 MW. No site location was disclosed and no operator primary document was retrieved; captured as an unverified lead.

- Ixian Infrastructure, Varpaisjarvi, Lapinlahti, Finland, event 11/17/26, single-source. A planned data center across 13 hectares targeting 50 MW, with scope to reach 150 MW; the two figures are distinct and are not blended. One trade press roundup citing Yle; the Yle original was not opened.

- Seen tonight and already captured, not new rows: the SpaceX linked 6 GW Cochise County, Arizona campus application (verified in October as finding 990; the Planning and Zoning Commission hearing is 12/09/26), and the AirTrunk Andhra Pradesh, Enlight Hof Shemen, and TIZA AI Gebeng items from prior runs.

PROJECT EVOLUTIONS

- Digital Realty Digital Park Fechenheim, Frankfurt, Germany, event 11/17/26, verified (filed under its power category in the database). The dedicated 110 kV underground connection is now operational, designed for up to 300 MVA, built over about 20 months. Campus plan: 11 data centers, up to 200 MW IT at full build-out, 3 operating, the fourth due in 2027. No Fechenheim row exists in production; the campus record is queued as a divergence for the quarterly census refresh.

- Dade County Industrial Park, Georgia, event 11/17/26, single-source. The county Industrial Development Authority withdrew its letter of intent tied to the proposed Masterworks Atlanta data center (about 300 MW in prior coverage) after the countywide moratorium below. The project is on hold.

- Seen tonight and already captured, not new rows: the Fermi Project Matador hyperscaler prepayment (verified finding 1655; tonight's touch records explicitly that the same 11/12/26 release terminated the TensorWave 222 MW lease and the AMD credit support, leaving Matador without a signed tenant), the Nebius Vineland slip to Q2 2027 (verified), the IREN Horizon equipment delivery delay, the AWS Hobart transformer transport delay, and the AWS Wheatfield groundbreaking of 11/12/26.

BLOCKERS

- No blocker was first seen tonight as its own row. The night's blocker substance is the Fermi Project Matador termination touch: the 11/12/26 Fermi release also terminated the TensorWave 222 MW lease and the AMD credit support agreement, leaving Project Matador with zero signed leases; the termination now sits on the verified prepayment finding's record, carried under PROJECT EVOLUTIONS above.

REGULATORY RESTRICTIONS

- Pitt County, North Carolina, LATE, event 11/16/26, verified. After the public hearing, the Board voted unanimously to adopt a two-year moratorium on data center development, tied to the county's first unified development ordinance, expected complete by the end of 2027. The Board stopped short of a ban. This resolves yesterday's watch finding.

- New Braunfels, Texas, LATE, event 11/16/26, verified. City Council approved ORD26-367 on second and final reading, unanimously. The final text substitutes a 3,000-foot setback for the earlier 2,000-foot figure and adds a decommissioning plan and a surety bond requirement, on top of heavy industrial zoning with a Type 2 special use permit and a ban over the Edwards Aquifer recharge zone. This resolves the watch finding carried since 11/13/26.

- Springfield, Missouri, LATE, event 11/16/26, single-source. Council voted unanimously to extend the data center administrative delay (in place since late June) to 02/24/27, and passed a substitute definition bill 6-2-1. A judge denied the developer bid to lift the moratorium on 11/09/26.

- Dade County, Georgia, LATE, event 11/05/26, single-source. The county approved a 90-day moratorium countywide after the roughly 300 MW Masterworks Atlanta proposal; procedural reporting on the vote conflicts and is recorded unresolved.

- United States (national), event 11/17/26, single-source. Members of Congress including Rep. McGovern rallied at the Capitol and delivered thousands of petitions demanding a national data center moratorium, backing the AI Data Center Moratorium Act. A political action, not an enacted restriction.

- Loudoun County, Virginia, event 11/17/26, watch. The pause vote sat on today's agenda as item 14.m (up to 12 months per application, about 33 pending applications); the meeting ran from 4:00pm EST and no outcome was public by run time. A county statement titled as an enactment that the gov rung surfaced was verified as the 09/16/26 statement on the September vote, not tonight's outcome. Checked again tomorrow.

- Salem, Oregon, event 11/17/26, watch. The special meeting on Resolution 2026-46, which would interpret the city code to exclude AI and hyperscale data centers and would apply to the Verrus Oakline at Mill Creek application, sits at 6:00pm PST tonight, after this run's search window. Checked tomorrow.

- Dedham, Massachusetts, event 11/16/26, watch. No Article 8 result (the proposed pause to 11/30/27) was found in town postings, local coverage, or X by run time; that is a retrieval outcome, not evidence the article passed or failed. Checked tomorrow.

- Seen tonight and already captured, not new rows: the Independence, Missouri 180-day moratorium approved 11/16/26 (verified, Nebius exempt), the Mesa County moratorium (verified; tonight's Land Development Code vote outcome was not reported at run time), and Sen. Hawley's national moratorium call of 11/11/26.

COMMUNITY ISSUES

- Sutton, Massachusetts, LATE, event 11/16/26, corroborated (touch on the existing finding). At the first Planning Board meeting on zoning for the 900 MW Kraft Group campus, board members put bylaw drafting at 6 to 10 months, longer than the May Town Meeting pitch, and the board is also weighing a one-year moratorium. The citizens petition is reported at hundreds of signatures; certification by the town clerk was not reported in any source retrieved, and no application has been filed.

- Botetourt County, Virginia (Google Greenfield), LATE, event 11/16/26, single-source (touch, moved to watch). After the merits hearing in the FOIA suit over the reported $3 billion campus performance agreement, the judge declined to rule, ordered supplemental briefs by Friday 11/20/26, and indicated a ruling could come as early as Monday 11/23/26, which is the finding's next review date.

- Olyphant, Pennsylvania (Project Triboro), event 11/17/26, corroborated (touch on the existing watch finding). Tonight's special meeting was set to consider settling the ERCOR lawsuit and approving the $101 million Community Benefits Agreement. New element: the Mid Valley School District filed for an injunction to stop the borough proceeding until the district can participate. The vote outcome was not reported by run time; review 11/18/26.

- xAI Southaven, Mississippi, LATE, event 11/13/26, corroborated. xAI and MZX Tech filed their answer in the NAACP Clean Air Act suit, admitting at least 27 temporary turbines were present in early 2026 with no PSD, state construction, or Title V permit for the temporary units, relying on the state exemption letter for trailer-mounted units, and admitting the turbines' NOx and formaldehyde emissions reach parts of Mississippi and Tennessee while denying significance and liability. The United States is now an intervenor-plaintiff.

- Red Oak, Texas, event 11/17/26, single-source. The Red Oak Say No More Data Center campaign organized a protest at tonight's joint City Council and Planning and Zoning meeting on rezoning more land for data centers, tied to its September notice lawsuit over the May rezoning of over 800 acres. The meeting outcome was not reported by run time.

- Oregon, Ohio, LATE, event 11/16/26, single-source. Council voted 6 to 1 to shrink the Capacity LLC land deal for the proposed Vantage campus (about 475 MW at full load) to about 63 acres for $4.13 million, 13 days after voters banned data centers over 25 MW and Vantage said the project will not move forward as proposed. Capacity may walk away by 07/31/27 and recover most of its deposit.

- Racine, Wisconsin, event 11/17/26, lead only. An X post reports a law firm won a suit forcing Racine to release its Microsoft water supply projections, and a judge ordered less redaction in a utility plan serving a Meta data center. No web grounding was completed; captured as an unverified lead and nothing more.

PERMITTING ISSUES

- Macquarie Engineering and Technology Campus, 2 Alma Road, Sydney, Australia, event 11/17/26, single-source. The SEARs planning filing was lodged for the 200 MW campus (42,015 sqm, about A$2 billion, timelines not shared). The campus was announced in July 2026 and is absent from production; its record is queued as a divergence for the quarterly census refresh.

- Salix, Iowa, event 11/17/26, lead only. An X post quoting The Journal reports Google is conducting a required traffic study as part of a data center assessment in Salix. The named article was not retrieved and no non-X source was found; captured as an unverified lead.

- Project Camellia, Effingham County, Georgia: the tabled site plan was due back today, 11/17/26, with a moratorium discussion also slated; no disposition was reported by run time in any lane. It is a follow-up for tomorrow, not a negative finding.

TIMELINE RISK

No timeline slips tonight.

FINANCING ITEMS

- HSBC sells Project Jupiter loan slice, Dona Ana County, New Mexico, LATE, disclosed 11/16/26, single-source. HSBC sold its roughly $300 million slice (under 2 percent) of Project Jupiter's $18 billion construction financing at prices in the mid-80s, below the 89 to 91 cent range quoted in September, following the Oracle force majeure notice. Oracle stock fell about 4 percent on 11/17/26. Bloomberg reporting relayed by one outlet; HSBC declined comment.

- ING and Societe Generale loan sales, event 11/17/26, single-source. The Financial Times reports ING's sale process includes about $500 million of loans linked to several operators and Project Jupiter, and Societe Generale has sought buyers for about $300 million tied to Project Lighthouse (Vantage, Port Washington) and Project Frontier (Vantage, Texas), quoted above 90 cents. Related to the open ING auction watch finding; tonight's item is the wider reported sale set.

text:
Softball Recap · Tue., Nov. 17 🥎

Texas Tech just named Tara Archibald its future head coach.

@TexasTechSB promoted the pitching coach behind back to back WCWS runs to co head coach today. She'll take over from Gerry Glasco, her father, whenever he retires.

Here's what else parents should know tonight 👇

🔸 TEXAS TECH SETS ITS SUCCESSION PLAN

Archibald has called pitches for All Americans NiJaree Canady and Kaitlyn Terry during back to back WCWS runs.

Before Lubbock: 135 and 97 in five seasons as Eastern Illinois head coach.

Glasco says there is no timetable for his retirement.

💡 Why it matters: when a coach is near the end of a career, ask who will be coaching your daughter by her junior year.

🔸 TEXAS TECH FLIPS AVA SALCEDO

The lefty outfielder from Washington (Okla.) High was committed to Oklahoma State. Today Texas Tech announced her signing for 2027.

Two state titles, four state track records, and travel ball with Oklahoma Athletics 18 National.

Tech's 2027 class is now five, led by catcher Hollynn Gentry (No. 11, Softball America/Rivals).

💡 Why it matters: a verbal is not a signature. Plans can change on both sides until the papers are signed.

🔸 RUTGERS SIGNS FOUR

Mia Camacho (Whittier Christian, Firecrackers Select) is the CIF Player of the Year and holds the Orange County home run record.

Also signed: Kendall Kemp, 6 foot 2 pitcher Ava Seeger (Impact Gold National Siegel) and Zoe Sheffield.

💡 Why it matters: Big Ten staffs recruit coast to coast. Camacho is moving from California to New Jersey.

🔸 UNLV SIGNS EIGHT

Kristie Fox added Sophia Debs, Brooklyn Dent, Sidney Kleiner, Sullivan McLaughlin, Tia Nichols, Briley Pinks, Riley Piorkowski and Payton Walling for 2027.

Nichols hit .507 with 13 home runs this spring. Six of the eight are from California.

💡 Why it matters: mid major classes are full of players from top clubs like Impact Gold, OC Batbusters and Firecrackers.

🔸 TEAM USA VS. JAPAN STARTS THURSDAY

Patty Gasso's national team has landed in Nagoya for a three game Japan All Star Series, Nov. 19 to 22.

Pitchers include Canady and Karlyn Pickens. UCLA's Aleena Garcia and Oklahoma's Kendall Wells are the two current college players on the roster.

💡 Why it matters: the national team pipeline runs straight through today's college rosters.

👇 Parents, when a program recruits your daughter, do you ask who will be coaching her in four years?

text:
Somewhere at Paycor Stadium, a man is halfway up a ladder with a giant letter E when he looks down and realizes his next assignment is spelling ICKEY WOODS. There isn’t an E big enough to fix that work order. 🪜🐅

Sunday night against Pittsburgh started with a particularly Cincinnati spelling test. The Bengals had announced AJ Greene, the football content creator, as Ruler of the Jungle. Folks here see “AJ Green” and reach for a No. 18 jersey. Fair enough. The former Bengals receiver even did the honors in 2023. Give the creator his E, give the receiver his flowers, and give the poor guy on the ladder a minute. He brought exactly one letter. If the next Ruler is Boomer Esiason, somebody better back a whole truck up to that ladder.

Then who gets the pregame honors? Ickey Woods. Of all the people in Cincinnati who could settle an identity question without saying a word, they found the guy who can do it with his feet.

That’s why my favorite guy in this cartoon is the second sign man. Look at his face. He’s had the ICKEY WOODS placard ready for a while. He could holler up and save his buddy a trip. He has apparently decided to let this play develop.

Down below, No. 30 has the Who Dey mic. The kid in the matching jersey has already picked up the Shuffle. Dad has committed both feet to a decision his knees were hoping to discuss first. Ickey, meanwhile, looks like he could carry that mic through a goal-line defense and still have enough room to dance. The man ran for 1,066 yards and 15 touchdowns as a rookie. He earned every single one of those steps.

I don’t know why the pregame lineup changed. The ladder is mine. The part where a whole lot of Cincinnati sees that white No. 30 and immediately knows what to do with its feet? That part pretty much draws itself.

And the final spelling lesson of the evening? Cincinnati 38, Pittsburgh 18. You can hang that one exactly as written. Preferably before the sign guy clocks out.

Who Dey, Ickey. Somebody hold that ladder. 🏈

@Bengals @THE_Ickster @Aj_greene15 @ajgreen_18 @steelers @SNFonNBC

Crystal Dynamics has another round of layoffs, the sixth round since 2020, when they shipped their last game Marvel Avengers🚀

✅Developers like UI software engineer Garin R. K. Richards, senior game designer Joshua Mitchell, and senior environment technical artist Kevin Baker sharing news of their job cuts on LinkedIn.

✅Three sets of cuts in 2025 alone following financial upheaval at parent company Embracer Group and the cancellation of Perfect Dark.

✅Laid-off artist Kevin Baker had integrated tools like Claude Code and procedural tech for upcoming projects like Tomb Raider: Catalyst, highlighting the studio's use of generative AI despite ongoing staff reductions.

✅Despite the continuous reduction in workforce, and previous broken assurances from Embracer Group that the studio would be unaffected, 

Crystal Dynamics maintains that it remains fully committed to their upcoming Tomb Raider games.

Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis is set to arrive February 12, 2027 and Catalyst would come after, but has been delayed after initially planning Legacy of Atlantis for 2026 and Catalyst for 2027.

text:
Here's the full statement.

November 17, 2026

Mayor Mamdani, Schools Chancellor Samuels Launch Technology in Schools Coalition Following Implementation of Nation's Broadest Generative AI Ban

Coalition to build on Public Schools' efforts to bring more human connection back to classrooms

Group will evaluate research, procurement strategies, national and international best practices to offer recommendations for technology use in classrooms

NEW YORK – Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani and New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) Chancellor Kamar Samuels today announced a continued pivot away from reliance on technology-based instruction with the launch of the Technology in Schools Coalition.

The coalition is a group of 70 educators, parent leaders, students, elected officials, advocates, union partners and experts. The group will provide recommendations by the end of June on how New York City Public Schools should – or should not – engage in technology-based instruction. Those recommendations will inform policy decisions for next school year.

“A strong education is about human connection, curiosity and the ability to work through difficult problems independently. That's exactly what we want to foster in classrooms across New York City. That is why, in September, we implemented a moratorium on generative AI for students in grades 2-K through eighth grade. As technology companies increasingly push the idea that AI can solve every challenge in our classrooms, we must remember that there is no substitute for a great teacher or the friendships that help young people learn and grow. The Technology in Schools Coalition will help guide our approach to these questions and ensure that decisions about our students’ education are shaped by the people who know our schools best. We look forward to working alongside teachers, parents, unions, education experts and others on the frontlines to build classrooms that put the needs of New York City students first," said Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

"In September, we set a new standard for protecting our students' data, learning, and critical thinking skills with our 2026-2027 AI and screen time policy. Today, with the announcement of the Technology in Schools Coalition, we continue to raise the bar for what responsive, community engagement looks like on this topic," said Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels. "Through the Coalition, NYC families, educators, and partners will directly shape our AI and screen time policy for next school year and beyond, ensuring their experiences and perspectives are accounted for. I look forward to working in partnership with the Coalition to keep our students safe and to protect their learning through responsible technology guardrails, and I’m grateful for their willingness to share their time and expertise on behalf of our students."

This group is a response to concerns from parents, educators, and elected officials, as well as a growing body of research on the dangers of excessive screen use and the cognitive offloading allowed by AI that affects negatively children's learning. Additionally, the coalition will explore whether research supports some targeted use of AI, such as learning a second language.

The group's first meeting will be in December.

"As a former teacher, I know the safety and education of our children is paramount, and any technology in our classrooms must be backed by peer-reviewed research. Convening this coalition is a good step in the right direction, and I look forward to working with the chancellor to keep our kids safe," said Councilman Eric Dinowitz, Education Chair.

“Technology cannot be blindly implemented into the education of our most impressionable minds. We must take a serious, informed approach before integrating evolving tech into our classrooms. A coalition comprised of local leaders and advocates is the community-centered approach we have called for. We look forward to the recommendations put forth by the coalition that ensures NYC remains a tech stronghold while not jeopardizing the educational experience of the largest public school system in the country,” said Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, Chair of the Committee on Technology.

“Technology in classrooms should be in service of advancing educational achievement and increasing students’ understanding of the world around them. If these tools are not properly stewarded, they can replicate systems of bias, exacerbate inequality, and lead to unknown risks for data privacy and learning outcomes. The use of educational technology must be guided by students, educators, and families to ensure they are serving our public school communities and not the profit-margins of tech corporations. I applaud Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYC Public Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels for implementing a moratorium on AI in schools through 8th Grade and establishing a task force that includes the voices of impacted community members to evaluate the use of technology in schools.” - NYS Senator Kristen Gonzalez (D-59), Chair of the Committee on Internet & Technology

"I spent more than two decades in the classroom. Teachers know what learning looks like. The wonderful look in a child's eye that follows necessary, productive struggle. It cannot be replaced by a screen," said Council Member Rita Joseph, Chair of the Higher Education Committee. "Our young people deserve classrooms that build critical thinking, curiosity, and real human connection. I applaud Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for putting educators, families, and students at the table, because the people who know our classrooms best should be the ones deciding what belongs in them."

“Students build strong educational foundations through dedicated teachers, evidence-based curriculum, meaningful human connection and the opportunity to learn and grow alongside their peers. AI must not undermine these essential parts of the classroom experience. Today’s announcement reflects Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels’ commitment to putting students’ education first. By bringing together experts who understand the day-to-day realities of our schools, they are ensuring that the people closest to our classrooms have a meaningful role in shaping how technology is used in our schools and how we educate the next generation." – Assemblyman Bobby Carroll, Chair of the Committee on Libraries and Education Technology

“The appropriate use of technology in our schools has been one of the main areas of concern and feedback raised by parents and school communities to the Panel for Educational Policy,” said Alan Ong.  “As Chair of the Panel, I applaud the opportunity to bring together stakeholders to engage in meaningful dialogue about how we can move our schools forward in this rapidly evolving technological landscape. I look forward to the Panel's role in this coalition and to working collaboratively with the Mayor, the Chancellor, and our school communities on this important topic.”

This builds on previous work by Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels to increase academic rigor in the school system including:

Developing and instituting the nation’s most aggressive policy on Artificial Intelligence
Launching free, high-quality 2-K for more than 2,000 families; expanding to 10,000 additional families next year
Continued investments in high-quality 3-K and pre-K, saving families thousands of dollars per year
Continued progress on reducing class size through focused planning and a $1.5B billion investment
Raising teacher pay
Dramatically improving procurement practices
Investing nearly $70 million into preschool education for students with disabilities
Expanding New York City Reads and New York City Solves
