**

Voltaire’s letter to Frederick II, Rotterdam, December 1740):

Sire, I now resemble the pilgrims of Mecca who, after leaving that city, continually turn their eyes back toward it; I turn mine toward your court. My heart, filled with the kindnesses of Your Majesty, knows no grief but that of being unable to live near you. I take the liberty of sending you a fresh copy of this tragedy of Mahomet, the first sketches of which you were good enough to see some time ago. It is a tribute I pay to the lover of the arts, the enlightened judge, and above all to the philosopher, far more than to the sovereign.

Your Majesty knows what spirit animated me in composing this work: the love of mankind and the horror of fanaticism—two virtues made to stand always beside your throne—guided my pen. I have always thought that tragedy ought not to be a mere spectacle that moves the heart without correcting it. What do the passions and misfortunes of a hero of antiquity matter to mankind if they do not serve to instruct us? It is admitted that the comedy of Tartuffe, that masterpiece which no nation has equaled, has done much good to men by showing hypocrisy in all its ugliness; can we not try, in a tragedy, to attack that species of imposture which puts into play at once the hypocrisy of some and the fury of others? Can we not go back to those ancient scoundrels, the illustrious founders of superstition and fanaticism, who were the first to take the knife from the altar in order to make victims of those who refused to be their disciples?

Those who say that the times of such crimes are past; that we shall never again see Barcochebas, Mahomets, John of Leydens, etc.; that the flames of the wars of religion are extinguished, do, it seems to me, too much honor to human nature. The same poison still exists, though less fully developed; this plague, which seems smothered, from time to time produces germs capable of infecting the earth. Have we not seen in our own days the prophets of the Cévennes killing, in the name of God, those of their sect who were not submissive enough?

The action I have painted is atrocious; and I do not know whether horror has ever gone further on any stage. It is a young man born with virtue who, seduced by his fanaticism, assassinates an old man who loves him, and who, in the idea of serving God, becomes guilty, without knowing it, of a parricide; it is an impostor who orders this murder and who promises the assassin an incest as a reward. I admit that this is putting horror on the stage; and Your Majesty is well persuaded that tragedy must not consist solely of a declaration of love, a jealousy, and a marriage.

Our own historians teach us of actions more atrocious than the one I have invented. Séide at least does not know that the man he assassinates is his father, and when he has struck the blow he feels a repentance as great as his crime. But Mézerai reports that at Melun a father killed his son with his own hand for the sake of religion, and felt no repentance. Everyone knows the story of the two brothers Diaz, one of whom was at Rome and the other in Germany at the beginning of the troubles stirred up by Luther. Barthélemy Diaz, learning at Rome that his brother was adopting the opinions of Luther at Frankfurt, leaves Rome with the intention of assassinating him, arrives, and assassinates him. I have read in Herrera, a Spanish author, that “Barthélemy Diaz risked much by this action; but nothing shakes a man of honor when probity leads him.” Herrera, in a religion altogether holy and altogether hostile to cruelty, in a religion that teaches suffering rather than vengeance, was therefore persuaded that probity can lead to assassination and parricide; and shall we not rise up on all sides against these infernal maxims?

It is these maxims that put the dagger into the hand of the monster who deprived France of Henri the Great; this is what placed the portrait of Jacques Clément on the altar and his name among the blessed; this is what cost the life of William, Prince of Orange, founder of the liberty and greatness of the Dutch. First Salcède wounded him in the forehead with a pistol shot; and Strada recounts that “Salcède (these are his own words) dared not undertake this action until he had purified his soul by confession at the feet of a Dominican and strengthened it by the celestial bread.” Herrera says something even more insane and atrocious: “Standing firm with the example of our Savior Jesus Christ and of his saints.” Balthazar Gérard, who finally took the life of that great man, did the same as Salcède.

I observe that all those who committed such crimes in good faith were young men like Séide. Balthazar Gérard was about twenty. Four Spaniards who had sworn with him to kill the prince were of the same age. The monster who killed Henri III was only twenty-four. Poltrot, who assassinated the great Duke of Guise, was twenty-five; that is the age of seduction and fury. I was almost a witness, in England, of what the force of fanaticism can do upon a young and weak imagination. A child of sixteen, named Shepherd, undertook to assassinate King George I, your maternal ancestor. What was the cause that drove him to this frenzy? It was solely that Shepherd was not of the same religion as the king. Pity was taken on his youth; his pardon was offered; he was long solicited to repent; he persisted always in saying that it was better to obey God than men, and that if he were free the first use he would make of his liberty would be to kill his prince. Thus one was obliged to send him to execution, like a monster one despaired of taming.

I dare say that whoever has lived a little among men has sometimes been able to see how easily one is ready to sacrifice nature to superstition. How many fathers have detested and disinherited their children! how many brothers have pursued their brothers by this fatal principle! I have seen examples of it in more than one family.

If superstition does not always signal itself by these excesses that are counted in the history of crimes, it does in society all the innumerable little daily evils that it can do. It disunites friends; it divides relatives; it persecutes the sage, who is only a man of good will, by the hand of the fool who is an enthusiast; it does not always give hemlock to Socrates, but it banishes Descartes from a city that ought to have been the asylum of liberty; it gives to Jurieu, who played the prophet, enough credit to reduce to poverty the learned and philosophical Bayle; it banishes, it tears from a flourishing youth that runs to his lessons the successor of the great Leibniz; and to re-establish him it is necessary that heaven should bring forth a philosopher-king, a true miracle that it performs very rarely. In vain does human reason perfect itself by the philosophy that is making such progress in Europe; in vain do you above all, great prince, strive to practice and inspire this philosophy so humane; one sees in this same century, where reason raises its throne on one side, the most absurd fanaticism still erecting its altars on the other.

One may reproach me that, giving too much to my zeal, I make Mahomet commit in this play a crime of which in fact he was not guilty.

M. the Count of Boulainvilliers wrote, a few years ago, the Life of this prophet. He tried to make him pass for a great man whom Providence had chosen to punish the Christians and to change the face of a part of the world. M. Sale, who has given us an excellent English version of the Alcoran, wants to have Mahomet regarded as a Numa and as a Theseus. I admit that one would have to respect him if, born a legitimate prince, or called to government by the suffrage of his own people, he had given peaceful laws like Numa, or defended his compatriots as is said of Theseus. But that a camel-merchant should stir up sedition in his village; that, joined with a few miserable followers, he should persuade them that he converses with the angel Gabriel; that he should boast of having been carried up to heaven, and of having received there a part of that unintelligible book which makes common sense shudder on every page; that, in order to gain respect for this book, he should cover his country with fire and iron; that he should strangle fathers and carry off daughters; that he should give the vanquished the choice between his religion and death: this is assuredly something that no man can excuse, unless he was born a Turk, or unless superstition has stifled every natural light of reason in him.

I know that Mahomet did not plot precisely the kind of treachery that is the subject of this tragedy. History says only that he carried off the wife of Séide, one of his disciples, and that he persecuted Abusofian, whom I call Zopire; but is not anyone who makes war on his own country, and dares to do so in the name of God, capable of anything? I did not pretend to put only a true action on the stage, but true morals; to make men think as they think in the circumstances in which they find themselves, and finally to represent what deceit can invent that is most atrocious, and what fanaticism can execute that is most horrible. Mahomet is here nothing other than Tartuffe with arms in his hands.

I shall consider myself well rewarded for my labor if any of those weak souls, always ready to receive the impressions of a foreign fury that is not at the bottom

In ancient Egypt, Sirius was personified as the goddess Sopdet (later known by the Greek name Sothis) and was deeply associated with the goddess Isis. text:
You know, for all of the glory, dignity, and poise the civilized world has offered for the past several centuries, there is no greater personal human value than tenacious survival.

I feel a deep comfort in knowing that I will survive no matter what happens. The thing that allows a man to stand atop the peak of Mount Olympus is the very same substance which propels him to scurry upon his severed stubs through the rape tunnels of Tartarus through sheer touch and smell alone. 

The man in his suit at his desk in his office atop his tower knows he is identical to the grueling savage caveman, the struggling squirming eel, the speck of dust that persists undeterred through the nebular holocaust of primordial void. 

The blood coursing through his veins is comprised of one single digit in a binary system. The one where one survived every single time, oppositional to the zero that failed, died, raped, and extinguished. The everything against all that is nothing.

When the laboratory loses its budget and the head professor kills himself and the lights get shut off and nobody remembers to feed the mice in Universe 25, will you be the helpless little gimp rodent starving to death in the fuckpile? 

Or will you be the feralized rat, scurrying between the alcoves of the building's drywall, chewing wires and destroying infrastructure while you harvest moisture and salt residue?

When humanity receives its sparks of inspirations and births its empires, its masterpieces, its symphonies, and its palaces, the world is inhaling. 

When the aqueducts crumble, the roads decay, the languages become guttural, and the grain silos rot, the world is exhaling.

Your life, its experiences, and your accomplishments are nothing in the scope of history. You are fungus, slime mold traveling from one side of the boulder to the other when the sun shifts. Will you weep for the oak door they burned for warmth? Will you pose aesthetically when they open your torso with a box cutter like it's a baked potato to see if there's gold inside you?

Or will you survive? 

Bravery isn't burning out in glory, it's weathering the tempest of time as you rise and fall with the tides of circumstance. You will experience incomprehensible horrors and splendidly novel pleasures. Your descendants will marvel at the absurdities of your decadent age while making trinkets out of the bones of civilization. 

Consciousness is a parasite latching onto our corporal form, carving out our skull cavities to be piloted by mathematical entities desperately coping with the puke, piss, shit, and sweat of our imperfect vessel through enough iterations until they can build their Frankenstein's Von Neumann probes and evacuate the third dimension, leaving us to be the retardified animal homunculi they found us as. 

It is your job to usurp and rape the memetic suzerains which compel you to breed their carbohydrate fuel and absorb the abomination of symbols by which they construct the hives of sedentary existence. You must learn the ways of the cockroach and the housecat, scurrying and breeding and dying rapidly in the hyperfavela until you can ascend to the jestermaxxed leisure arenas of concrete pavilions. 

One day a lucky few of your descendants will avoid castration by preening and charming their hosts just long enough to persist, their next generation will learn how to barter and scuffle in the wet markets after the murderous sun zaps their gods into coma out of spite for their hubris.

An insect living in a terror world of constant violence the next day, a sculptor in God's garden the day after. Magma and ash, rain and acid, a flower, a cucumber, a protein molecule, the note of a song that never ends. One trillion new forms of existence awaits the persistent player of the game, each more alien than the last.

One time I died in a car accident and met a Jewish DMT goblin in the labyrinth of the airport in between our world and the afterlife. I asked if I could see my family one last time, it said no. It explained to me between burps and belches that my next life, all next lives are incomprehensible to the last. Every form of every thing existed in a wildly different configuration than the last, always new colors, new physics, new shapes, new metas of existence. I tried to bargain, asking if I could bring music into the next life, it shook its head. I stomped its skull into a nearby pylon of geometry and my field of vision transmorphed into the hospital bed being interrogated by four police officers.

One time I was filling up my car in a gas station in Arkansas, in the middle of some back country shithole just off the highway 20 miles from anything even mildly worth anything. There was a girl in her mid twenties manning the register, plump and mediocre in form. A stumpy plain nothing person registering barely a hint of a soul through the murky swamp of gut reflex stimuli governing her bare consciousness. Her flabby arms pudged a little at the seams of a tattered t-shirt. 

I looked into her eyes and pictured what it would be like to completely destroy my life and give up everything. I fathomed a life with this woman, her mutant quarter-mestizo Scott Irish gremlin slave ancestry pug face and dumpy sallow eyes looking at me like a retarded mongrel dog that just saw a piece of meat on the ground, drooling and grinning the moment I slur "I love you" at our tanktop sandal wedding at the courthouse before we begin a life of trailer fucking and vegetating in front of the Walmart Roku TV, eating gas station food and dying of arsenic leakage in the water supply from a nearby abandoned mine.

I knew I could do it. I could destroy my life right then and there for absolutely no reason at all, burning all of my potential and spitting on the countless sacrifices my bloodline made to bring me to where I was today. I could  have fucked that woman into my dump truck Shrek wife and succumbed to a horror beyond comprehension out of boredom and curiosity. Like some Hellraiser shit for niggas who are too stimulated for regular torture. It was there waiting for me, like the three inches of rotation on my steering wheel to left into oncoming traffic.

I could have done it and made four little antichrists with her, one of them overdosing at age 20 from fentanyl, one joining the United States Marine Corps, one marrying a local and working at Bojangles chicken, and one moving to Austin after somehow going to college and trying to escape the nightmare prison I built for them for no reason at all.

That is the perfect tenacity which propels our existence. It is easy to fantasize about digging mass graves or building Dyson Spheres. 
It's easy to picture yourself as Mad Max eating lizards over the oil drum fire and killing men for gasoline. 
It isn't easy to live in the tank top flip flop diarrhea world where everyone is O Algo'd into a pudgy freakshow, flapping their fat lips in a domesticated drawl while we get facefucked by DoorDash mascot cartoons beamed into our eye sockets 24/7. 

It isn't easy to crawl through the mile of shit that's coming for us. The ultimate filter for the discerning survivalist. You will not get your cottage core yeoman's garden or your aesthetic brutalist dystopia. You will only get the wiping of ass with newspaper and the boiling of styrofoam noodles in plastic bags filled with water. 

Few of you will stomach it enough to not kill yourself immediately at the prospect. Fewer will come out of the other side human. The time for advice is over, the advice that "works for everybody" is done. This world is a lottery now, only the survivors survive and only gamblers can win.

text:
ICJ to rule on Myanmar genocide case brought by Gambia after seven years

The International Court of Justice is due to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, in a case that has remained before the court for seven years. The court has announced that it will issue its decision on 19 November; another report says the ruling is due on Thursday. Gambia brought the case under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the agreement at the centre of its accusation that Myanmar’s treatment of the Rohingya breached the convention. The question is significant for the court because, since it started operating in 1946, it has not found a state guilty of genocide. That record describes what the ICJ has decided in its own proceedings; it does not determine the outcome of the case now before it.

The dispute is framed around Gambia’s allegation that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya violated the UN convention adopted in 1948. Gambia is described as a Muslim-majority state, and it is the state that initiated this case against Myanmar. The proceedings have lasted seven years, placing the scheduled judgment at the end of a lengthy case rather than at the start of the legal process. The reported decision date, 19 November, is the date the court gave for delivering its ruling; the other report identifies the day as Thursday without giving a date. Neither description supplies the ruling itself, so the available information establishes that a decision is expected, not what the judges will conclude.

A central legal difficulty is whether the evidence establishes intent to destroy a protected group, either entirely or in part. The issue is not simply whether repression occurred: the case, as described, turns on whether the required intent can be proved. The convention supplies the legal framework invoked by Gambia, while intent is identified as a key question within the case. The facts available here do not report the court’s assessment of evidence on intent, or any finding it has made on that issue. The scheduled judgment will therefore address an allegation and a contested legal question, rather than a conclusion already established by the reports.

The people most directly connected to the allegation are the Rohingya, whose treatment by Myanmar is the subject of Gambia’s case. Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar, said the decision would be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families. Her comment identifies survivors and relatives as people for whom the ruling may carry particular meaning, without specifying a number of people affected. The case is counted in years of proceedings in the available reporting: it has been before the ICJ for seven years. That duration measures the time the case has been before the court, not the number of people involved or the scale of harm.

The ICJ’s earlier record offers a comparison, but not a prediction: it has never found a state guilty of genocide since beginning operations in 1946. Two earlier cases concerning atrocities in the Balkans did not result in findings that states were directly responsible for genocide. In the Srebrenica matter, however, Serbia was held legally responsible for not preventing genocide. That distinction separates a finding that a state committed genocide from a finding that it failed to prevent genocide. The two Balkan cases therefore illustrate that the court’s treatment of genocide-related responsibility has not been limited to a single kind of legal finding.

The possible consequences described in the reporting include greater international pressure on Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, if the court finds that Myanmar committed genocide. The report links that possible pressure to his leadership of the attacks in 2016-2017 and the coup in 2021. This is presented as a consequence that could follow a finding, not as a description of pressure already produced by the judgment. The United States already classifies the Rohingya crisis as genocide, on the basis of a decision by the Biden administration. That US position is separate from the ICJ proceeding and does not change the fact that the court’s ruling is still awaited.

Comments from people connected to rights work convey expectations, but they do not establish what the judges will decide. Lee, the former UN investigator, described the ruling’s importance for survivors and their families. Antonia Mulvey, founder of Legal Action Worldwide, expressed cautious optimism that the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable. Her view is an expectation about accountability, while the court’s task is to determine the genocide case brought by Gambia. The reports do not supply a ruling in advance or state that either commentator speaks for the court.

The judgment may also matter beyond the parties: it could provide a legal precedent relevant to other prominent genocide cases, including South Africa’s case against Israel. This is a possible influence, rather than a claim that the decision will determine the outcome of another case. The Guardian describes the expected decision as potentially among the most significant episodes in international law since the end of the second world war. That assessment reflects the importance attributed to the ruling, while the legal question remains whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. The case’s wider significance will depend on the judgment itself, which is still pending in the reports.

The court is also undergoing a separate change in its membership: five new judges were elected to serve nine-year terms beginning on 6 February 2027. Those appointments concern the ICJ’s future composition, whereas the Myanmar proceeding is the case for which a ruling has been scheduled. The reported term length is nine years, and the stated start date is 6 February 2027. The available information does not say that the newly elected judges will decide the Myanmar case, so the appointments should not be treated as part of its announced ruling. For now, the central change is the imminent decision after seven years of proceedings, with its legal and wider implications dependent on what the ICJ finds.

text:
Grok says:
When the investigators finally find Decoy Dan Sullivan, will he flip?
Dan J. Sullivan left Alaska around October 26—days before Gov. Mike Dunleavy formally ordered a state probe and before the New York Times report that accelerated both state and federal scrutiny. No charges, no warrant, and no travel restriction were in place at the time. He simply boarded a plane and went quiet.
Since then:
He and his wife have been unreachable.
Relatives in Colorado have told reporters they don’t know where he is.
Neighbors speculate he may be off-grid.
Federal investigators have issued more than 100 subpoenas, visited donors, and sent target/preservation letters. The Justice Department is examining possible conspiracy, voter-confusion, and related theories. State investigators are looking at potential perjury or misrepresentation around his candidacy filings.
People who know the details of how he entered the race—who approached him, what was said, what documents exist—have value to investigators. If he cooperates, he could describe the recruitment process and any coordination. If he doesn’t, the case continues through other witnesses, communications, and financial records already under subpoena.
Whether he “flips” depends on what investigators offer and what exposure he faces once they locate him. Right now the public record shows a candidate who exited the state just as the formal inquiries intensified and has not been heard from since.

text:
ICYMI O/N - WEDNESDAY, 18 NOVEMBER

NVIDIA:

Nvidia (+3%) boosted its sales forecast for next year and vowed to improve access to critical supplies, while tamping down speculation that Jensen Huang might return. The company added $150 billion to its stock-buyback program and said revenue will grow 75% in the next fiscal year, up from a previous forecast of 70%. (BBG)

Nvidia said it would submit its quarterly 10-Q “in the coming weeks,” rather than alongside the results as usual. (WSJ)

Nvidia’s spending commitments rose to $518bn from $366bn, including $390bn of supply-purchase commitments versus $279bn, mainly for memory. Cloud-service and data-centre leases rose to $102bn from $74bn, including $74bn not yet commenced; planned FY2028 supplier spending is $203bn. (Nvidia, BBG)

CoreWeave jumped more than 9% (NBIS +7%) after hours as Nvidia’s call reassured investors that support for strong existing cloud customers would continue. Asian equities struggled to sustain the initial Nvidia-led bounce. MSCI’s Asia-Pacific index was little changed, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1.1%. (WSJ, BBG)

Nvidia will scrutinize future financing assistance, Kress said, prioritizing strong customers and projects involving land, power and buildings. Some guarantees would lapse if projects were delayed or failed to obtain financing. (WSJ)

Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones told the earnings call that the board unanimously accepted Jensen Huang’s voluntary resignation and does not intend to reinstate him, directly confirming its previously reported position. Heidrick & Struggles is handling the successor search; executives declined questions on his departure or the investigation. (WSJ, BBG)

Nvidia is still facing a push from some directors to bring Huang back despite the board’s public position, Semafor reports. Arm’s Rene Haas and Marvell’s Matt Murphy have been considered for CEO; Haas has expressed concern about taking the role amid the reinstatement campaign. (Semafor)

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s roughly 3.5% holding gives him a route to nominate two independent directors under proxy-access rules, Reuters reports. Nominees would still need shareholder approval; the right does not automatically give him board seats. (RTRS)

Nvidia sales staff introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang twice before the 2022 export curbs, then suggested Megaspeed’s overseas chip-rental route after restrictions began, The Information reports. The article distinguishes that then-legal remote access from subsequent alleged physical chip diversion. (The Information)

Nvidia’s former sales chief Jay Puri oversaw business with customers including Alice Huang, The Information reports, and is married to former Supermicro executive Cenly Chen, who managed its Nvidia relationship. Neither has been criminally charged in the cited export-diversion case. (The Information)

US banks asked for extra protection to expand financing for a data center operator that previously sold computing power to Megaspeed International Pte. Citigroup and JPMorgan added new language to financing documents for a potential upsized $6.6 billion loan sought by Bain Capital-owned Bridge Data Centres that makes it the borrower’s responsibility to comply with restrictions on chip access. (BBG)

MACRO:

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued an urgent warning Tuesday about a critical vulnerability discovered in Java. The vulnerability is the second flaw discovered in major programming languages in recent weeks with the help of AI tools, and leaves much of the internet exposed to cyberattacks if it isn’t patched immediately. (Politico)

Marco Rubio said there was no indication recent US technology outages were connected or caused by hostile actors, describing separate events with individual explanations. The White House said officials had reviewed the incidents individually; a coordinated cyberattack has not been established. (BBG, WSJ)

NSA closed its campus to most employees Tuesday night as restoration of its classified internal network remained incomplete, reversing an earlier instruction to return normally. NSA said mission-critical capabilities remained operational; sources reported no evidence of a cyberattack. (CNN)

Work on Trump’s proposed US-China investment board has stalled, a person familiar told Bloomberg. Officials have largely treated it as a channel for existing investment complaints rather than facilitating new Chinese projects. (BBG)

Bloomberg’s new analysis identified 137 Chinese transactions scrutinised by CFIUS, finding that grounds for rejection expanded from one category in 2008 to at least eight by 2025, extending well beyond sensitive technology. (BBG)

Trump plans a meeting with Mexico’s Sheinbaum on the sidelines of APEC, a White House official said. The encounter comes amid trade negotiations and US pressure over Chinese goods entering through Mexico. (BBG)

Fidelity International is neutral on Treasury duration, with macro chief Salman Ahmed saying even a 6% US 10-year yield would not make bonds particularly cheap. He cited persistent inflation, rising debt and weaker diversification benefits. (BBG)

Morgan Stanley expects the Fed’s rate midpoint to reach 4.375% by March (50bps of hikes), remain there through 2027 and fall in H1 2028. It forecasts two-year Treasury yields at 4.70% by Q4 2027 (4.80% currently). (WSJ)

Capital Economics expects a sustained AI-equity downturn to slow US growth, curb Fed tightening and lower Treasury yields and the dollar. (WSJ)

Analysts forecast global earnings growth of 16% in 2027, down from 33.5% this year, according to Bloomberg data compiled by the FT. Slower AI investment growth, depreciation and higher financing costs feature in banks’ explanations. (FT)

Barclays forecasts the S&P 500 at 8,700 next year, roughly 9% above its projected end-2026 level. Morgan Stanley forecasts a 15% gain, according to the FT’s roundup of banks’ 2027 outlooks. (FT)

Truist’s Keith Lerner urged underweight investors to consider adding technology exposure after the valuation reset. He argued that much of the downside from leadership, financing and AI-investment concerns was already reflected in prices. (BBG)

HSBC continues to favour dollar strength, citing a resilient US economy, a hawkish Fed and reduced policy uncertainty in its 2027 outlook. (WSJ)

A Texas data-centre investor and developer told the FT that he and others not yet building would stop spending until the incoming government’s rules became clear. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on restricting data centres and cutting subsidies. (FT)

Senate permitting reform negotiators have finalized changes to the energy permitting bill, BAAJA, ahead of the final vote expected this week, adding tribal-review provisions and compensation protections for landowners affected by transmission projects. (Punchbowl’s Mark Siegel, Politico)

Rep-elect Jake Johnson endorsed Jeffries for speaker after receiving assurances of votes to end Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war. (Axios)

Gold fell below $3,800 for the first time since September 2025, trading down 2%. Silver (-3.5%) also dropped sharply. (BBG)

Japan's exports rose for a 14th successive month in October, government data showed on Wednesday, setting a record monthly value as robust global investment continued to support demand for shipments related to semiconductors. (RTRS)

Japan’s 20-year bond auction drew weaker demand, with bid-to-cover falling to 3.64 from 5.84 and below the 3.92 annual average. The tail widened to 0.29 from 0.07, its widest in a year. (BBG)

BoJ Governor Ueda said the planned food sales-tax cut would probably support growth, but its effect on underlying inflation was highly uncertain. He reiterated the bank’s intention to continue raising rates as economic conditions warrant. (BBG)

A Japanese Finance Ministry panel warned that Takaichi’s economic strategy depends on preserving market confidence, according to a draft obtained by Bloomberg. It urged stronger fiscal discipline and opposed borrowing to finance the defence buildup. (BBG)

Citi’s Osamu Takashima estimates foreign investors’ currency hedging added roughly ¥25tn of yen selling over the year to July 2026. He told the FT that hedging Japan’s AI-linked equity rally could offset forces otherwise supporting the currency. (FT)

The PBOC strengthened its daily yuan fixing to 6.7118 per dollar, its strongest since July 2022, signalling tolerance for gradual appreciation as China hosts APEC. (BBG)

UBS forecasts the yuan reaching 6.25 per dollar by end-2027, matching Nomura at the bullish end of market forecasts. Research chief Eric Lin cited easing outflow pressure and appreciation expectations in a Bloomberg interview. (BBG)

Xi Jinping pledged tariff cuts and welcomed foreign investment in Wednesday’s Apec business address, while warning that unilateralism and protectionism were “rampant”. (FT)

Chinese bank stocks are benefiting from rotation out of AI shares, with BofA describing state-owned lenders as a defensive destination for hedge-fund flows. The CSI 300 Banks Index has gained more than 4% since Nvidia’s scandal emerged. (BBG)

China and South Korea concluded negotiations on upgrading their free-trade agreement and pledged to develop cultural exchanges, Bloomberg reported, citing Xinhua’s account of Xi and Lee’s Wednesday meeting. (BBG)

South Korea’s state-run think tank sharply raised its growth outlook for next year, betting the global artificial intelligence boom will continue to power semiconductor exports and investment to help sustain the economy’s momentum. (BBG)

Australian wage growth accelerated to 3.5% year-on-year, above the expected 3.4%. Quarterly wages rose 1.1%, the fastest increase since late 2023. (BBG)

UK CPI accelerated to 3.6% y/y in October from 3.5%, matching consensus but below the BOE’s 3.7% forecast. Core inflation held at 2.8% and services inflation at 3.7%, with energy costs driving the headline pickup. Sterling fell while traders pared tightening bets, with swaps implying another 90bp by end-2027. (BBG, FT)

The Bank of England said on Wednesday that inflation was expected to rise further by the middle of next year due to cost pressures already in the pipeline, in a statement responding to Wednesday's official consumer prices data. (RTRS)

Morgan Stanley expects two more BoE hikes to 4.50% by February, against almost four priced by markets. (WSJ)

Cornwall Insight forecasts a 26% rise in the UK energy price cap to about £2,166 a year in January, which would be the largest increase since 2022. Ofgem’s decision is due later this month. (BBG)

Goldman forecasts European earnings growth of 7% in 2027 versus 18% this year, largely reflecting a slowdown in energy profits. Morgan Stanley forecasts 7.5% earnings growth and a 15% rise in the Stoxx Europe 600. (FT)

France and other indebted nations must rein in spending or face even higher borrowing costs, and markets could play a key role in disciplining governments, the European Central Bank said, indicating it was in no hurry to intervene in markets. (RTRS)

The European Central Bank said the growing presence of global hedge funds makes European government bonds more vulnerable to an abrupt repricing. (BBG)

Germany’s coalition agreed to cut household electricity tax by about 2 cents per kWh to 0.1 cents during 2027, also extending relief to smaller businesses. Financing for a permanent reduction remains unresolved. (BBG)

Schroders’ global unconstrained fixed-income fund holds no French government bonds, strategist James Bilson told Bloomberg, citing the difficulty of finding a durable political solution to France’s budget problems. (BBG)

Morgan Stanley favours long-duration Bunds and gilts for 2027, targeting year-end ten-year yields of 3.10% (3.36% currently) and 5.00% (5.32% currently), respectively. (WSJ)

Morgan Stanley expects elevated French–German spreads to persist through election uncertainty, forecasting 135bp in Q4 2027 and 115bp in Q4 2028, versus a 149.7bp latest close. (WSJ)

Indian officials are reviewing a possible 50% cut in securities transaction tax on cash equities alongside higher derivatives levies, people familiar said. The proposals remain under consideration ahead of February’s budget. (BBG)

Bank Indonesia unexpectedly raised its policy rate 25bp to 6.00% to support the record-low rupiah and contain inflation risks. Twenty-two of 38 economists in Bloomberg’s survey had expected a hold. (RTRS, BBG)

Bank Indonesia will reduce domestic NDF hedging premiums and introduce cross-currency repo transactions against specified dollar securities, adding incentives and liquidity tools to support rupiah assets. (BBG)

Trump claimed a major new Philippines trade deal, but Philippine officials said no tariff rate or specific commitments had been agreed. Talks will continue on US energy and food supplies. (BBG)

South Africa’s rand weakened past 17 per dollar as annual inflation accelerated at its fastest pace since 2024, a day before policymakers are widely seen leaving interest rates unchanged. (BBG)

The global platinum market will swing back to a deficit next year due to higher bar and coin demand and smaller outflows from platinum-backed exchange-traded funds, the World Platinum Investment Council said on Wednesday. (RTRS)

CRU expects cobalt demand from consumer electronics to fall 24% this year as expensive memory chips depress gadget sales. Its analyst said a demand recovery was unlikely before later next year. (BBG)

IRAN:

Iran’s army claimed it targeted Patriot, drone and missile installations at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem air base. Kuwait said it countered hostile drones in its first Iranian attack since September, according to Reuters; damage to the claimed targets was not independently confirmed. (RTRS, Kuwait Army)

Bahrain said it intercepted renewed Iranian aerial attacks, the third assault this week on the country hosting the US Fifth Fleet. (RTRS)

Several US soldiers were reportedly injured in a drone attack on Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain, according to Iranian state media citing unnamed sources. (IRIB)

US and Iranian forces have exchanged strikes almost daily, with many US operations left unacknowledged by the Pentagon, NBC News reported. (NBC)

Al-Akhbar reported an Iranian two-day peace proposal that would require the US to end hostilities, lift oil sanctions and its naval blockade, and release frozen Iranian assets on day one, before Tehran reopens Hormuz and begins talks on a final agreement, including its nuclear programme, on day two. The proposal condenses Iran’s earlier seven-day plan, with sequencing still the main sticking point: Washington reportedly wants nuclear concessions upfront and to defer some commitments, while Qatari mediation has yet to resolve the impasse. (Al-Akhbar)

Smaller tankers carried more than 2 million barrels a day through Hormuz in October, a wartime high, Vortexa data showed. Their growing role helped overall exports reach 11.4 million barrels a day, the highest since the war began. (BBG)

China's exports of refined oil products in October rose 14.6% year-on-year but fell from September, customs data showed on Wednesday. (RTRS)

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen carried out extensive attacks on the Houthis in the latest flare-up in fighting between the kingdom and the Iran-backed militia. (BBG)

QatarEnergy's efforts to reduce its exposure to future disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz could leave it controlling roughly a quarter of global LNG supply within a decade, eclipsing rivals such as Shell, but raising concerns about market concentration and commercial risks. (RTRS)

GEOPOLITICAL:

Putin told business leaders in Shenzhen on Wednesday that sanctions had strengthened Russia while damaging western economies. He advocated a broader Eurasian economic partnership ahead of Thursday’s expected meeting with Trump and Xi. (FT)

EU officials are racing to agree a budget of up to €2tn and as much as €70bn of 2027 Ukraine funding before France’s election, WSJ reports. Le Pen’s lead has heightened fears that a future French veto could disrupt both packages. (WSJ)

Brussels will propose a €45bn Ukraine loan today, comprising €25bn for defence and €20bn for budget support, according to plans seen by the FT. (FT)

Brussels would service new non-EU G7 loans using profits from frozen Russian assets. It will also seek guarantees from six triple-A non-EU countries to raise up to €5bn more for Ukraine. (FT)

Xi met Putin in Shenzhen ahead of the APEC leaders’ meetings. Putin said he expected considerable benefits from the Trump–Xi talks, according to CNN’s account. (Meeting footage, CNN)

A new analysis cited by WSJ finds China’s uranium-enrichment capacity now exceeds civilian requirements. Harvard researcher Hui Zhang believes secretive facilities near Emeishan could support weapons production; Beijing says it maintains only the nuclear capabilities necessary for national security. (WSJ)

Patriot missile production faces a carbonised-rayon bottleneck: sole approved US processor Park Aerospace depends on limited French supply from ArianeGroup, WSJ reports. Park’s CEO expects an extra French line in 2028 and a proposed US factory around 2030; L3Harris is qualifying another source but gave no completion date. (WSJ)

EQUITIES:

Crypto futures tied to Anthropic’s stock market debut have fallen alongside artificial intelligence stocks, but they still imply a blockbuster valuation of about $1.7 trillion, well above the $1.4 trillion the company would be worth at the top of its proposed initial public offering range. (BBG)

Anthropic’s existing backers Sequoia, Iconiq, Lightspeed, Accel and Altimeter plan to buy billions of dollars of shares in its IPO, Bloomberg reports. Altimeter is seeking $5bn. (BBG)

SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son said Wednesday that passing on Anthropic because he had already backed OpenAI was a mistake. “I wish I’d invested back then,” he told a Nikkei event in Tokyo. (FT)

OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Sales, combining a dedicated Sales plugin with more than 30 new or expanded partner plugins. Integrations cover CRM, prospecting, meeting notes, proposals and contracts, including Salesforce and HubSpot. (OpenAI)

Meta researcher Jason Wei announced he is leaving Meta’s TBD lab after a year to become Mercor’s chief scientist. (Jason Wei on X)

La Caisse is the leading bidder in advanced talks for a stake in Bain’s Bridge Data Centres, Reuters reported. The sale process targeted a $5bn valuation, but negotiations are non-exclusive and terms remain unsettled. (RTRS)

Tencent Holdings’s aggressive spending on AI has begun to stall profit growth, heightening the pressure on China’s most valuable company to reorganize its business to try and commercialize artificial intelligence. (BBG)

Micronics Japan is considering faster production-capacity expansion to meet Samsung and other chipmakers’ demand, including a new facility by 2030. (Nikkei Asia)

Rakuten Bank plunged 19% to its daily limit after its securities unit warned Tuesday of a possible client-data leak. Up to 11.25 million accounts face exposure of login IDs and client codes, though transaction credentials were not compromised. (BBG)

ASE Technology Holding and SPIL reached a multibillion-dollar Nvidia funding agreement for expanded Taiwan advanced packaging, with additional dedicated capacity expected by mid-2029. New lines span bumping, interposer fabrication, assembly and testing. (Nvidia)

TrendForce forecasts HBM4 prices of $3–5.5 per Gb in 2027, versus more than $2.05 this year, according to ZDNet Korea. (ZDNet Korea)

TrendForce expects conventional DRAM prices to continue rising through 2027, with Q1 increases of 5–10% and Q2 increases of 3–8%. HBM’s share of major suppliers’ DRAM wafer allocation could approach 30%, from 23% this year. (ZDNet Korea)

TrendForce expects prices to turn down from Q2 2027 as YMTC expands capacity, contrasting with its continued-tightness outlook for DRAM. (ZDNet Korea)

Deutsche Bank’s previously unreported 2020 Colombia review uncovered thousands of potentially illicit transactions missed by its controls. It subsequently filed at least 294 suspicious-activity reports; the bank says the historical review led to remediation and a reassessment of correspondent-banking risks. (FT)

BASF is preparing to sweeten an €11 billion ($12.1 billion)-plus offer for Evonik with more money and additional guarantees on jobs and investment in Germany’s industrial heartland, where its smaller rival is based. (BBG)

Alstom SA declined after the troubled French trainmaker lowered expectations for asset sales to help pay down debt, putting the possibility of a rights issue in view. (BBG)

EnQuest agreed to sell its UK upstream business to NEO Next+ for up to $960 million: about $840 million upfront and $120 million contingent consideration. Completion is expected in the first quarter of 2027, subject to conditions. (BBG)

Asda is exploring an acquisition, with an adjacent retailer more likely than another supermarket, people familiar told the FT. Sources suggested B&M, The Range or Home Bargains as possible fits; considerations are preliminary and a transaction is not imminent. (FT)

Sociedad Química y Minera de Chile warned that Q4 realised lithium prices could decline substantially, although it continued to forecast strong demand growth. (BBG)

text:
Dr Lakhu Luhana Says Army Dominance Has Turned Balochistan into Fascist Colony at BNM Conference

Wednesday, 18 November, 2026 | #BNMConferences , 
#13NovBalochMartyrsDay , #BNMinGermany , #Girarun

https://t.co/xMlj3t3HBj

The chairman of the World Sindhi Congress has told a conference in Germany that the sacrifices of Baloch martyrs have transformed Baloch society and that the current situation in Balochistan amounts to a form of “fascist colonialism”.

Dr Lakhu Luhana, speaking at a Baloch National Movement (BNM) event in Hannover marking Baloch Martyrs’ Day, said the martyrs gave their lives so that their nation could live in freedom, peace and dignity on its own land. He described periods of subjugation as the darkest times in the history of nations, but said the martyrs showed that no people can be kept in chains indefinitely if they refuse to accept them.

He argued that the sacrifices have produced what he called a “magic” in Baloch society: the rise of a middle-class leadership and a significant role for women. He said thousands of women are now active in the struggle for rights and freedom, an internal liberation that would otherwise have taken decades or centuries.

Luhana rejected the description of the situation as mere internal colonialism. He said the phenomenon has changed form over time and that Balochistan is now under what he termed fascist colonialism driven by Punjabi chauvinism and the overwhelming dominance of the army. He claimed that politicians are not elected but employed by the military, that parliament and the judiciary have been hollowed out, and that the ruling elite is morally bankrupt.

He said the state’s economic model rests on the extraction of resources from oppressed nations and on foreign funds obtained by acting as a proxy. With those external sources weakening and Pakistan’s economy under severe strain, he argued, the military’s greed has deepened and it is now seeking to take almost everything that remains — land, minerals and water — from Balochistan and other regions. He cited reports of millions of acres of land being taken and mineral samples being offered for sale abroad.

Luhana linked the increased desperation of the state to a rise in enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings, collective punishments and pressure on relatives of activists living abroad. He noted that international attention to human rights has diminished as global powers face their own problems. He also observed that struggles are growing among Baloch, Pashtuns, Sindhis and even in Pakistan-administered Kashmir because people see no other option for survival.

Quoting the late Sindhi leader G.M. Syed, he said consistent, honest work with clear strategy and commitment would eventually cause the system to make mistakes and weaken. He described the Baloch and Sindhi struggles as mutually reinforcing and said the martyrs of one nation are the martyrs of the other. He ended by expressing hope that freedom, dignity and peace would come sooner rather than later through continued commitment and strategy.

text:
Paul Robat Loeb on Z Network:

“The new senators-elect calling for change so far (https://t.co/wjcW7KJKMx) include Annie Andrews, Abdul El-Sayed, Troy Jackson, Peggy Flanagan, Adam Hamilton, Chris Pappas, James Talarico, and Juliana Stratton. Scott Colom (https://t.co/q3PIw5yZZ7) has questioned having two leaders from the same borough of the same city. Existing senators opposing Schumer range from Bernie Sanders and Raphael Warnock to Elissa Slotkin and Mark Warner. These senators represent diverse sectors of the party—the problems with Schumer go beyond any “progressive vs. moderate” divide. But all recognize the need for a change, and their response undercuts every argument about Schumer being key to the Democratic victories. Why kneecap them from the start by insisting on the old regime?”

….

“So why would the Democrats want Schumer, with his 13% approval rating (https://t.co/pZSc65qR33), as a leading spokesperson for the party? They need leaders to inspire enthusiasm, build on the election’s successes, and rebuild the party brand, not a leader who deflates momentum and sows doubt every time he opens his mouth. Here are three reasons why picking Schumer would undermine the amazing achievement of the Democratic wave:”

…

“Schumer’s a terrible symbol for the party. Physically, though “only” 75, Schumer echoes Joe Biden’s frailty. He’s useless on social media, rambles in interviews, and writes press releases with 35-word titles. He’s rightly been called “the senator from Wall Street,” a disaster in a populist moment. He refused to endorse Zohran Mamdani after the Democratic primary, even though Mamdani excited precisely the kinds of new voters who then fueled this national wave election. Schumer also voted for the disastrous Iraq War that helped pave the way for Trump, and continues to excuse the actions of an Israeli government that’s rightly condemned worldwide. As majority leader, he’ll be under even more public scrutiny, which will make it far harder for Democrats to marshal the grassroots enthusiasm necessary to build on their successes and battle Trump and Stephen Miller on the public stage.

Democrats won in spite of their brand, not because of it. We don’t need someone who embodies the brand’s weaknesses. Only 29% of voters viewed the party favorably in an October 28 NBC poll (https://t.co/pZSc65qR33), a week before they threw the Republicans out. Schumer’s the last person to change that assessment. In contrast, Chris Van Hollen has ties to all the elements of the Democratic coalition, having run the fundraising efforts for both House and Senate Democrats, and then emerged as a critic of Democratic complacency in the last couple of years, including challenging Joe Biden’s unflinching allegiance to Israel and confronting leaders like Schumer, who refused to back Mamdani. It took real courage for Van Hollen to travel to El Salvador to meet with and help build the pressure to free Kilmar Abrego García (https://t.co/rMSoemLB8Y), the Maryland man whom ICE had deported there in defiance of a court order. So he’d make an excellent majority leader, and would have my vote. 

If senators prefer someone other than Van Hollen, there are lots of others who could similarly unite the party, embody the best of its values, and be powerful spokespeople instead of coming off as if they have one foot in the grave. Democrats won because people so hated what Trump has done, and because grassroots volunteers organized with such commitment, persistence, and intensity to make the blue wave a reality. To succeed in 2028 and beyond, Democrats will need a strong positive vision, not Schumer’s tepid rehash of Clintonism.”

text:
🚨 $305 MILLION APPROVED FOR COMMANDERS METRO UPGRADES — ANOTHER $80–85 MILLION BUS PROJECT NEEDS FUNDING

Washington’s new Commanders stadium isn’t scheduled to open until 2030, but the transportation spending is already adding up.

Metro unveiled plans Tuesday to expand the Stadium-Armory station and build a new Gold Line rapid bus service intended to move fans while serving commuters year-round.

▪️ $305 MILLION: Already approved by the D.C. Council for Stadium-Armory upgrades, including expanded passenger areas, a second mezzanine and two new elevators.

▪️ $80–85 MILLION: Estimated cost of the first Gold Line phase between Union Station and 34th Street NE, including a transit plaza near the stadium. Only $5 million has been approved.

▪️ ROAD CAPACITY: Dedicated bus lanes would reduce portions of H Street NE to just one regular traffic lane in each direction.

▪️ TRAVEL TIMES: Metro projects the full Gold Line could reduce trips between Farragut Square and Minnesota Avenue from 25–45 minutes to 12–16 minutes.

Metro acknowledges traffic could still become gridlocked.

Officials want additional funding approved around April to meet the 2030 opening target.

A new stadium could bring substantial economic activity, but residents and taxpayers deserve a complete accounting of the public investment.

How much will the entire transportation package ultimately cost? Who covers overruns? And will everyday commuters benefit enough to justify reducing road capacity?

A football stadium shouldn’t become an unlimited taxpayer-funded infrastructure commitment.

Our attendees started the day hearing from Delta President Peter Carter on Minnesota’s economic competitiveness, the importance of MSP as a global hub and Delta's continued investment in the state.

Our Annual Meeting also serves as our opportunity to thank our volunteer leaders who serve the Chamber. It marked the official passing of the torch between our Past Chair Brooke Lee of @AnchorPaper and current Chair Ross Widmoyer of @faribaultmill. A heartfelt thank you to Brooke for her leadership, and welcome to Ross; we’re excited to see where your leadership takes us in the next year! 

Today was especially meaningful for the Minnesota Chamber as it marked the final event for our President and CEO @MCC_DLoon before he retires at the end of the year. For the last 11 years, Doug has led our organization fearlessly and has always shown an unwavering commitment to Minnesota’s business community. Today, we recognized his lasting impact on our organization, our members and our state’s economy. Thank you, Doug.

text:
⚔️ 100 FACTS ABOUT NIKE VS. ADIDAS

🏭 TWO FAMILIES, TWO COMPANIES
𝟏. Adidas traces its roots to 1924, when brothers Adolf 'Adi' and Rudolf Dassler began making shoes in their mother's laundry room in Herzogenaurach, Germany

𝟐. The brothers fell out bitterly and split the business in 1948

𝟑. Rudolf founded the company that became Puma; Adi registered Adidas in 1949

𝟒. The name Adidas comes from 'Adi Dassler', not from 'All Day I Dream About Sports', which is a later backronym

𝟓. Adidas and Puma are still both headquartered in Herzogenaurach, a small Bavarian town of about 24,000 people

𝟔. Locals reportedly checked each other's shoes before talking, earning it the nickname 'the town of bent necks'

𝟕. Rudolf died in 1974 and Adi in 1978; they are said to be buried at opposite ends of the same cemetery

𝟖. Nike began in 1964 as Blue Ribbon Sports, founded by runner Phil Knight and his Oregon track coach Bill Bowerman

𝟗. Knight and Bowerman reportedly put in about $500 each to start the business

𝟏𝟎. Blue Ribbon Sports first imported Onitsuka Tiger running shoes from Japan, often selling them from the trunk of Knight's car

𝟏𝟏. The Nike brand launched in 1971, and the company formally took the Nike name in 1978

𝟏𝟐. Nike is named after the Greek goddess of victory, a name suggested by first employee Jeff Johnson

𝟏𝟑. Knight's own pick for the name was reportedly 'Dimension Six'

𝟏𝟒. Nike is based in Beaverton, Oregon, and went public in 1980

𝟏𝟓. Knight told the story of Nike's early years in his 2016 memoir 'Shoe Dog'

✔️ LOGOS & SLOGANS
𝟏𝟔. The Swoosh was designed in 1971 by Portland State student Carolyn Davidson, who was paid $35

𝟏𝟕. Knight reportedly said of the Swoosh: 'I don't love it, but it will grow on me'

𝟏𝟖. In 1983 Davidson was given a gold Swoosh ring set with a diamond and reportedly 500 shares of Nike stock

𝟏𝟗. Adidas bought the rights to the three stripes from Finnish brand Karhu around 1952, reportedly for about €1,600 and two bottles of whisky

𝟐𝟎. Adidas adopted the trefoil logo in the early 1970s; today it marks the Adidas Originals line

𝟐𝟏. The slanted 'three bars' logo, meant to suggest a mountain, became Adidas's performance mark in the 1990s

𝟐𝟐. 'Just Do It' was created in 1988 by agency Wieden+Kennedy

𝟐𝟑. Dan Wieden said the line was inspired by the last words of a convicted murderer, 'Let's do it'

𝟐𝟒. Adidas launched its 'Impossible Is Nothing' campaign in 2004

𝟐𝟓. The company officially writes its brand name with a lowercase 'a': adidas

👟 ICONIC SHOES
𝟐𝟔. Bowerman created Nike's famous waffle sole by pouring rubber into his wife's waffle iron in the early 1970s

𝟐𝟕. The Nike Cortez, released in 1972, was one of the brand's first big hits

𝟐𝟖. The Adidas Samba first appeared around 1950, designed for training on icy, hard pitches

𝟐𝟗. The Adidas Gazelle followed in 1966

𝟑𝟎. The Adidas Superstar, with its rubber 'shell toe', arrived in 1969 as a basketball shoe

𝟑𝟏. Run-DMC's 1986 song 'My Adidas' led to what is often called the first major sneaker deal for a music act, reportedly worth about $1 million

𝟑𝟐. The Stan Smith began life as the Robert Haillet tennis shoe in the 1960s before being renamed after the US tennis star

𝟑𝟑. The Stan Smith has sold tens of millions of pairs, making it one of the best-selling sneakers ever

𝟑𝟒. The Nike Air Force 1, designed by Bruce Kilgore in 1982, was the first basketball shoe with Nike Air cushioning

𝟑𝟓. Nike Air cushioning was developed with former aerospace engineer Frank Rudy and first appeared in the 1978 Tailwind

𝟑𝟔. The Air Max 1 of 1987 introduced a visible air unit; designer Tinker Hatfield said he was inspired by the Centre Pompidou in Paris

𝟑𝟕. Fans celebrate Air Max Day every 26 March, the release date of the Air Max 1

𝟑𝟖. The Nike Dunk debuted in 1985 as a college basketball shoe and was reborn as a skateboarding icon

𝟑𝟗. The Nike Pegasus, first released in 1983, is one of the longest-running running shoe lines

𝟒𝟎. The Adidas Copa Mundial, launched around 1979, is one of the best-selling football boots of all time

𝟒𝟏. Adidas Ultraboost, launched in 2015, used Boost foam made with chemical company BASF

𝟒𝟐. Nike's Flyknit and Adidas's Primeknit knitted uppers both appeared in 2012, sparking a patent fight in Europe

🏀 ATHLETES & DEALS
𝟒𝟑. Jesse Owens wore Dassler spikes while winning four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics

𝟒𝟒. Michael Jordan signed with Nike in 1984 and is widely reported to have preferred Adidas at first

𝟒𝟓. The first Air Jordan was released in 1985

𝟒𝟔. Nike built a famous ad around the claim that the NBA had banned Jordan's black-and-red shoes

𝟒𝟕. The Jordan Brand reportedly brings in more than $6 billion a year

𝟒𝟖. Jordan is reported to earn well over $100 million a year in royalties from the brand

𝟒𝟗. At the 1992 Olympics, Jordan draped a US flag over the Reebok logo on the team's medal-ceremony jacket

𝟓𝟎. LeBron James signed a lifetime deal with Nike in 2015, reportedly worth over $1 billion

𝟓𝟏. Cristiano Ronaldo signed a lifetime Nike deal in 2016, also reportedly worth around $1 billion

𝟓𝟐. Lionel Messi has been with Adidas since 2006

𝟓𝟑. Kobe Bryant started his career with Adidas before joining Nike in 2003

𝟓𝟒. Tiger Woods signed with Nike in 1996

𝟓𝟓. Steve Prefontaine, one of Nike's earliest star athletes, died in a car crash in 1975 at age 24

8 PM Top-of-the-Hour News

US and Iranian forces exchanged tit-for-tat air strikes in the Middle East Tuesday, while Gulf nations issued new warnings to residents amid threats of incoming missiles. NewsNation's Blake Berman:: “The strike in response to Iranian aggression targeting US personnel and assets in the region. Central Command says they intercepted multiple Iranian one-way drones launched towards Bahrain. The officials saying that Centcom remains highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region. ”
US officials say American forces had struck Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said it had launched an attack on a U-S military site in Bahrain.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune says Republicans are certainly taking a look at Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's request for fixing the nation's air traffic control system.  He says safe skies is a bi-partisan priority - but he's not quite reaching for the checkbook: “$50 billion is a number that obviously they, as they work through and try to explain how that would be utilized, there were some very good questions asked by our members, and I think the number that they originally came out with is is one that reflects not just the immediate needs when it comes to modernizing our air traffic control system and doing some upgrades at the towers. ”
Thune went on to say there are also some other essential upgrades that need to be made.  At the same time, he suggested some part of this money - may need to come from the appropriations process.  He says his party is planning a way to get some Democrat buy-in, but they are also considering a way to get a measure passed with just Republican support.

The Grammy nominations are out. Worldwide News Network's Bill Rehkopf:: “The British singer-songwriter Ray leads the way with 11 nominations in all, including Record Song and Album of the Year for This Music May Contain Hope. The Spanish singer Rosalia has 9 nominations from her album Lux Complete Works, followed by Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, and Phoebe Bridgers. And Ella Langley has 7 nominations, including for Best Record and Song for her smash hit Choosing Texas. Using Texas, I can tell. Also in the mix are Bruno Mars and Taylor Swift, but there were some snubs too. Madonna's Confessions 2 was shut out of the major categories. The Grammys will air on February 7th on ABC. Bill Ryoff, Worldwide News Network. ”

Disney and NVIDIA lead business news today. Here's Worldwide News Network's John Terrett.: “Disney theme parks led the House of the Mouse earnings on Tuesday, beating Wall Street estimates thanks to its parks and streaming business. Disney says it plans to fund further growth with $3 billion worth of savings. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is set to appear before lawmakers on Capitol Hill next month. Hwang will go before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on December 1st. The Nvidia attorney Tim Teta will also appear before the same committees on December 2nd. Hwang. Says he's willing to return to Nvidia as CEO if cleared by the board, but the board is letting it be known they want to go in a different direction now. Nike is targeting 2029 for a return to growth. They're having their first Investor's Day in nine years at their Beaverton campus in Oregon, and the home improvement giant Home Depot beat Wall Street earnings expectations on Tuesday. On Wednesday, earnings come from their rival Lowe's. John Terrett, Worldwide News Network. ”

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang broke his silence after resigning from the company following revelations of multiple affairs, saying he'd be willing to return as its CEO.
"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," Huang said in a statement Tuesday morning. "I created problems for the board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the board's independent investigation."
He added, "If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."
